title: Chapter 18 — Future Condition Of Three Races In The United States
paragraphs: The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Three Races Which Inhabit the Territory of the United States

I have now completed the main task I set for myself. I have shown, as well as I could, the laws and the customs of American democracy. I could stop here, but the reader might feel that I have not met his expectations.

The absolute supremacy of democracy is not the only thing one finds in America; the inhabitants of the New World can be viewed from more than one angle. In the course of this work my subject has often led me to mention the Native Americans and Black Americans, but I have never been able to stop and show what place these two races hold within the democratic people I was describing. I have said in what spirit and under what laws the Anglo-American Union was formed, but I could only glance at the dangers that threaten that confederation, and it was equally impossible for me to give a detailed account of its chances of lasting, apart from its laws and customs. When I spoke of the united republican States, I made no guesses about whether republican forms would endure in the New World. And when I often referred to the commercial activity that prevails in the Union, I could not inquire into the future condition of the Americans as a commercial people.

These subjects are connected with my topic only indirectly, without being part of it. They are American without being democratic, and my main aim has been to portray democracy. I therefore had to put these questions off, and I now take them up as the fitting end of my work.

The territory now occupied or claimed by the American Union stretches from the shores of the Atlantic to those of the Pacific Ocean. To the east and west, its limits are those of the continent itself. To the south it reaches nearly to the tropics, and to the north it extends into the icy regions. The human beings scattered over this space do not form, as in Europe, so many branches of the same stock. At first glance one can pick out three races among them, naturally distinct and, I might almost say, hostile to one another. Education and law, as well as origin and outward appearance, had raised almost insurmountable barriers between them. But fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not blend, and each race fulfills its destiny apart.

Among these widely different families of men, the first to attract attention, superior in intelligence, power, and enjoyment, is the white or European, the preeminent man. Below him, in lower ranks, come the Black American and the Native American. These two unfortunate races have nothing in common: not birth, not features, not language, not habits. Their only likeness lies in their misfortunes. Both hold an inferior rank in the country they inhabit; both suffer under tyranny; and if their wrongs are not the same, they come, at any rate, from the same authors.

If we reasoned from what goes on in the world, we might almost say that the European is to the other races of mankind what man is to the lower animals. He makes them serve his purposes, and when he cannot subdue them, he destroys them. Oppression has, at one stroke, stripped the descendants of Africans of almost all the privileges of humanity. The Black American in the United States has lost all memory of his country. The language his forefathers spoke is never heard around him. He gave up their religion and forgot their customs when he ceased to belong to Africa, without gaining any claim to European privileges. So he remains halfway between the two communities, sold by one and rejected by the other, finding no spot in the universe to call his country, except the faint image of a home that his master’s roof provides.

The Black American has no family; woman is merely the temporary companion of his pleasures, and his children are his equals from the moment they are born. Should I call it a proof of God’s mercy or a visitation of his wrath, that in certain conditions man seems insensible to his extreme wretchedness, and almost develops a perverse fondness for the cause of his misfortunes? The Black American, plunged in this abyss of evils, scarcely feels his own calamitous situation. Violence made him a slave, and the habit of servitude gives him a slave’s thoughts and desires. He admires his tyrants more than he hates them, and finds his joy and pride in servile imitation of those who oppress him. His understanding has been degraded to the level of his soul.

The Black American enters slavery the moment he is born. Indeed, he may have been bought in the womb and begun his slavery before he began his existence. With no wants and no enjoyments, and useless to himself, he learns with his first ideas of existence that he is another man’s property, that this man has an interest in keeping him alive, and that the care of his life does not fall to himself. Even the power of thought appears to him a useless gift of Providence, and he quietly enjoys the privileges of his degradation. If he becomes free, he often finds independence a heavier burden than slavery. For he has learned in the course of his life to submit to everything except reason, and he knows too little of her dictates to obey them. A thousand new desires beset him, and he lacks the knowledge and energy to resist them. These are masters that must be fought, and he has learned only to submit and obey. In short, he sinks to such a depth of wretchedness that while servitude brutalizes him, liberty destroys him.

Oppression has been no less fatal to the Native Americans than to Black Americans, but its effects are different. Before white men arrived in the New World, the inhabitants of North America lived quietly in their woods, going through the changes of fortune, and practicing the virtues and vices, common to savage nations. The Europeans scattered the tribes, drove them into the wilderness, and condemned them to a wandering life full of inexpressible sufferings.

Savage nations are governed only by opinion and custom. The Native Americans lost their sense of attachment to their country; their families were dispersed, their traditions obscured, and the chain of their memories broken. All their habits were changed, and their wants grew beyond measure. European tyranny made them more disorderly and less civilized than they had been before. The moral and physical condition of the tribes kept getting worse, and they became more barbarous as they became more wretched. Nevertheless, the Europeans have not been able to transform the character of the Native Americans. They have had the power to destroy them, but they have never been able to make them submit to the rules of civilized society.

The lot of the Black American lies at the extreme limit of servitude, while that of the Native American lies at the farthest edge of liberty. Slavery does not produce more fatal effects on the first than independence does on the second. The Black slave has lost all property in his own person, and he cannot dispose of his own existence without committing a kind of fraud. But the savage is his own master as soon as he is able to act. He scarcely knows parental authority; he has never bent his will to that of any other person, nor learned the difference between voluntary obedience and shameful subjection; and the very name of law is unknown to him. To be free, for him, means to escape every shackle of society. He delights in this barbarous independence and would rather die than give up the least part of it, so civilization has little power over him.

The Black American makes a thousand fruitless efforts to work his way in among men who reject him. He conforms to the tastes of his oppressors, adopts their opinions, and hopes by imitating them to become part of their community. He has been told from infancy that his race is naturally inferior to the whites, and he accepts the claim and is ashamed of his own nature. In each of his features he finds a trace of slavery, and if it were in his power, he would gladly rid himself of everything that makes him what he is.

The Native American, on the contrary, has an imagination swollen with the supposed nobility of his origin, and he lives and dies amid these dreams of pride. Far from wanting to conform his habits to ours, he loves his savage life as the distinguishing mark of his race, and he rejects every step toward civilization, perhaps less from hatred of it than from dread of resembling the Europeans. *a He has nothing to set against our perfection in the arts but the resources of the wilderness, and nothing to set against our tactics but undisciplined courage. Our carefully worked-out plans are met only by the spontaneous instincts of savage life. Who can wonder if he fails in this unequal contest?

a [ The native of North America holds on to his opinions and even the most insignificant of his habits with a tenacity that has no parallel in history. For more than two hundred years the wandering tribes of North America have been in daily contact with the whites, and they have never taken from them either a custom or an idea. Yet the Europeans have had a powerful influence over the savages: they have made them more licentious, but not more European. In the summer of 1831 I happened to be beyond Lake Michigan, at a place called Green Bay, which serves as the farthest frontier between the United States and the Native Americans on the northwestern side. There I met an American officer, Major H., who talked to me at length about the inflexibility of the Native American character and then related the following fact: “I formerly knew a young Indian,” he said, “who had been educated at a college in New England, where he had greatly distinguished himself, and had acquired the external appearance of a member of civilized society. When the war broke out between ourselves and the English in 1810, I saw this young man again; he was serving in our army, at the head of the warriors of his tribe, for the Indians were admitted among the ranks of the Americans, upon condition that they would abstain from their horrible custom of scalping their victims. On the evening of the battle of . . ., C. came and sat himself down by the fire of our bivouac. I asked him what had been his fortune that day: he related his exploits; and growing warm and animated by the recollection of them, he concluded by suddenly opening the breast of his coat, saying, ‘You must not betray me — see here!’ And I actually beheld,” said the Major, “between his body and his shirt, the skin and hair of an English head, still dripping with gore.”]

The Black American, who earnestly wishes to mingle his race with the European, cannot do so, while the Native American, who might succeed to a certain extent, disdains even to try. The servility of the one dooms him to slavery; the pride of the other dooms him to death.

I remember that while I was traveling through the forests that still cover the State of Alabama, I came one day to the log house of a pioneer. I did not want to go into the American’s home, so I withdrew to rest for a while by a spring not far off in the woods. While I was there (it was near the Creek territory), a Native American woman appeared, followed by a Black woman and holding by the hand a little white girl of five or six, whom I took to be the pioneer’s daughter. A kind of barbarous luxury adorned the Native American woman’s dress: metal rings hung from her nostrils and ears; her hair, decorated with glass beads, fell loose on her shoulders; and I saw that she was not married, for she still wore the necklace of shells that a bride always lays on the marriage bed. The Black woman was dressed in shabby European clothes. All three came and sat down on the bank of the spring. The young Native American woman took the child in her arms and gave her the fond caresses a mother gives, while the Black woman tried by various small tricks to attract the attention of the young Creole.

In her slightest gestures the child showed a consciousness of superiority that contrasted strangely with her childish weakness, as if she received the attentions of her companions with a kind of condescension. The Black woman sat on the ground before her mistress, watching her smallest wishes, and seemingly torn between strong affection for the child and servile fear. The savage, in the midst of her tenderness, showed an air of freedom and pride that was almost ferocious. I had approached the group and was watching them in silence, but my curiosity probably displeased the Native American woman, for she suddenly rose, pushed the child roughly away from her, and, giving me an angry look, plunged into the thicket. I had often happened to see people of the three races that populate North America gathered in the same place. I had noticed in many different ways the preponderance of the whites. But in the scene I have just described there was something especially touching. A bond of affection united the oppressors with the oppressed here, and nature’s effort to bring them together made the immense distance that prejudice and law had placed between them all the more striking.
The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Native American Tribes Which Inhabit the Territory Possessed by the Union

Gradual disappearance of the native tribes — How it takes place — The miseries that accompany the forced migrations of the Native Americans — The savages of North America had only two ways of escaping destruction: war or civilization — They are no longer able to make war — Why they refused to become civilized when it was in their power, and why they cannot become so now that they want to — The example of the Creeks and Cherokees — The policy of the individual States toward these tribes — The policy of the Federal government.

None of the Native American tribes that once lived in the territory of New England — the Naragansetts, the Mohicans, the Pecots — exists any longer except in human memory. The Lenapes, who received William Penn on the banks of the Delaware a hundred and fifty years ago, have disappeared; and I myself met the last of the Iroquois, who were begging for alms. The nations I have named once covered the country all the way to the seacoast, but today a traveler must go more than a hundred leagues into the interior of the continent to find a Native American. These wild tribes have not only withdrawn; they have been destroyed. *b And as they give way or perish, an immense and growing people takes their place. There is no recorded instance of such prodigious growth or such rapid destruction, and it is not hard to describe how the destruction takes place.

b [ In the thirteen original States there are only 6,273 Native Americans remaining. (See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 90.) [The decrease is now far greater, and is verging on extinction. See page 360 of this volume.]]

When the Native Americans were the only inhabitants of the wilds from which they have since been driven out, their wants were few. They made their own weapons, their only drink was the water of the brook, and their clothes were the skins of the animals whose flesh fed them.

The Europeans brought firearms, strong liquor, and iron to the savages of North America. They taught them to exchange manufactured cloth for the rough garments that had satisfied their untutored simplicity before. The Native Americans had acquired new tastes without the skills to satisfy them, so they had to turn to the whites’ workmanship. But in return for these goods the savage had nothing to offer except the rich furs that still abounded in his woods. Hunting therefore became necessary, not only to feed himself but to obtain the only goods he could supply to Europe in barter. *c While the natives’ wants were thus increasing, their resources kept shrinking.

c [ In their Report to Congress on February 4, 1829, p. 23, Messrs. Clarke and Cass put it this way: “The time when the Indians generally could supply themselves with food and clothing, without any of the articles of civilized life, has long since passed away. The more remote tribes, beyond the Mississippi, who live where immense herds of buffalo are yet to be found and who follow those animals in their periodical migrations, could more easily than any others recur to the habits of their ancestors, and live without the white man or any of his manufactures. But the buffalo is constantly receding. The smaller animals, the bear, the deer, the beaver, the otter, the muskrat, etc., principally minister to the comfort and support of the Indians; and these cannot be taken without guns, ammunition, and traps. Among the Northwestern Indians particularly, the labor of supplying a family with food is excessive. Day after day is spent by the hunter without success, and during this interval his family must subsist upon bark or roots, or perish. Want and misery are around them and among them. Many die every winter from actual starvation.”

The Native Americans will not live as Europeans do, and yet they can neither survive without them nor live exactly as their fathers did. A fact that I likewise give on official authority shows this. Some members of a tribe on the banks of Lake Superior had killed a European. The American government forbade all trade with the tribe the guilty men belonged to until they were handed over to justice. The measure had the desired effect.]

As soon as a European settlement is formed near the territory the Native Americans occupy, the game animals take alarm. *d Thousands of savages wandering through the forests with no fixed dwelling did not disturb them. But as soon as they hear the continuous sounds of European labor nearby, they begin to flee and retreat to the West, where their instinct tells them they will find deserts of immeasurable extent. “The buffalo is constantly receding,” say Messrs. Clarke and Cass in their Report of the year 1829; “a few years since they approached the base of the Alleghany; and a few years hence they may even be rare upon the immense plains which extend to the base of the Rocky Mountains.” I have been assured that the approach of the whites is often felt in this way at two hundred leagues’ distance from their frontier. Their influence thus reaches tribes whose names are unknown to them, and who suffer the evils of usurpation long before they know who is responsible for their distress. *e

d [ “Five years ago,” says Volney in his “Tableau des Etats-Unis,” p. 370, “in going from Vincennes to Kaskaskia, a territory which now forms part of the State of Illinois, but which at the time I mention was completely wild (1797), you could not cross a prairie without seeing herds of from four to five hundred buffaloes. There are now none remaining; they swam across the Mississippi to escape from the hunters, and more particularly from the bells of the American cows.”]

e [ You can easily confirm what I am saying here by consulting the tabular statement of the Native American tribes living in the United States and its territories. (Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, pp. 90–105.) It shows that the tribes in the center of America are rapidly decreasing, even though the Europeans are still at a considerable distance from them.]

Bold adventurers soon move into the country the Native Americans have abandoned. When they have advanced about fifteen or twenty leagues beyond the outermost frontier of the whites, they begin building homes for civilized beings in the middle of the wilderness. This is done without difficulty, because the territory of a hunting nation is poorly defined. It is the common property of the tribe and belongs to no one in particular, so no individual interests are involved in protecting any part of it.

A few European families, settled in different places at a considerable distance from one another, soon drive away the wild animals that remain between their homes. The Native Americans, who had lived in a kind of abundance, then find it hard to survive, and harder still to obtain the goods for barter that they need.

Driving away their game deprives them of their means of existence, just as effectively as if our farmers’ fields were struck with barrenness. They are reduced, like starving wolves, to prowl through the abandoned woods looking for prey. Their instinctive love of their country attaches them to the soil that gave them birth, *f even after it has stopped yielding anything but misery and death. In the end they are forced to give in and leave. They follow the tracks of the elk, the buffalo, and the beaver, and these wild animals guide them in choosing their future country. Strictly speaking, then, it is not the Europeans who drive away the native inhabitants of America; it is famine that forces them to withdraw. This is a happy distinction that escaped the casuists of former times, and we owe it to modern discovery!

f [ “The Indians,” say Messrs. Clarke and Cass in their Report to Congress, p. 15, “are attached to their country by the same feelings which bind us to ours; and, besides, there are certain superstitious notions connected with the alienation of what the Great Spirit gave to their ancestors, which operate strongly upon the tribes who have made few or no cessions, but which are gradually weakened as our intercourse with them is extended. ‘We will not sell the spot which contains the bones of our fathers,’ is almost always the first answer to a proposition for a sale.”]

It is impossible to imagine how much suffering these forced emigrations involve. A people already exhausted and reduced undertake them, and the countries the newcomers go to are inhabited by other tribes, who receive them with jealous hostility. Hunger follows behind them, war awaits them ahead, and misery besets them on every side. Hoping to escape such a host of enemies, they separate, and each individual tries to find the means of supporting his existence in solitude and secrecy, living in the vastness of the wilderness like an outcast in civilized society. The social tie, which distress had long since weakened, then dissolves. They have lost their country, and soon their people desert them. Their very families are wiped out; the names they bore in common are forgotten; their language dies; and every trace of their origin disappears. Their nation has ceased to exist, except in the memory of the antiquaries of America and a few scholars of Europe.

I would be sorry if my reader supposed that I am coloring the picture too strongly. I saw with my own eyes several of the cases of misery I have described, and I witnessed sufferings I have no power to portray.

At the end of the year 1831, while I was on the left bank of the Mississippi at a place the Europeans named Memphis, a numerous band of Choctaws arrived (or Chactas, as the French in Louisiana call them). These savages had left their country and were trying to reach the right bank of the Mississippi, where they hoped to find the refuge the American government had promised them. It was the middle of winter, and the cold was unusually severe. The snow had frozen hard on the ground, and the river was carrying huge masses of ice. The Native Americans had their families with them, and they brought in their train the wounded and the sick, newborn children, and old men on the verge of death. They had neither tents nor wagons, only their weapons and some provisions. I watched them embark to cross the mighty river, and that solemn sight will never fade from my memory. No cry, no sob was heard among the assembled crowd; all were silent. Their calamities were of long standing, and they knew them to be beyond remedy. The Native Americans had all stepped into the boat that was to carry them across, but their dogs remained on the bank. As soon as these animals saw that their masters were leaving the shore for good, they set up a dismal howl and, plunging all together into the icy waters of the Mississippi, swam after the boat.

The ejection of the Native Americans very often takes place today in a regular and, so to speak, legal manner. When the European population begins to approach the edge of the wilderness inhabited by a savage tribe, the government of the United States usually sends envoys to them. The envoys gather the Native Americans on a large plain, eat and drink with them first, and then address them in the following way: “What have you to do in the land of your fathers? Before long, you must dig up their bones in order to live. In what respect is the country you inhabit better than another? Are there no woods, marshes, or prairies, except where you dwell? And can you live nowhere but under your own sun? Beyond those mountains which you see at the horizon, beyond the lake which bounds your territory on the west, there lie vast countries where beasts of chase are found in great abundance; sell your lands to us, and go to live happily in those solitudes.” After saying this, they lay out before the eyes of the Native Americans firearms, woolen garments, kegs of brandy, glass necklaces, tinsel bracelets, earrings, and mirrors. *g If, after seeing all these riches, the Native Americans still hesitate, it is hinted that they have no means of refusing the consent that is demanded, and that the government itself will soon be unable to protect their rights. What are they to do? Half convinced and half forced, they go to live in new deserts, where the importunate whites will not let them stay in peace for ten years. This is how the Americans obtain, at a very low price, whole provinces that the richest sovereigns of Europe could not buy. *h

g [ See, in the Legislative Documents of Congress (Doc. 117), the account of what happens on these occasions. This curious passage comes from the report mentioned above, made to Congress by Messrs. Clarke and Cass in February, 1829. Mr. Cass is now the Secretary of War.

“The Indians,” says the report, “reach the treaty-ground poor and almost naked. Large quantities of goods are taken there by the traders, and are seen and examined by the Indians. The women and children become importunate to have their wants supplied, and their influence is soon exerted to induce a sale. Their improvidence is habitual and unconquerable. The gratification of his immediate wants and desires is the ruling passion of an Indian. The expectation of future advantages seldom produces much effect. The experience of the past is lost, and the prospects of the future disregarded. It would be utterly hopeless to demand a cession of land, unless the means were at hand of gratifying their immediate wants; and when their condition and circumstances are fairly considered, it ought not to surprise us that they are so anxious to relieve themselves.”]

h [ On May 19, 1830, Mr. Edward Everett stated before the House of Representatives that the Americans had already acquired by treaty, to the east and west of the Mississippi, 230,000,000 acres. In 1808 the Osages gave up 48,000,000 acres for an annual payment of $1,000. In 1818 the Quapaws gave up 29,000,000 acres for $4,000. They kept for themselves a territory of 1,000,000 acres as a hunting ground. A solemn oath was taken that it would be respected, but before long it was invaded like the rest. Mr. Bell, in his Report of the Committee on Indian Affairs, February 24, 1830, has these words: “To pay an Indian tribe what their ancient hunting-grounds are worth to them, after the game is fled or destroyed, as a mode of appropriating wild lands claimed by Indians, has been found more convenient, and certainly it is more agreeable to the forms of justice, as well as more merciful, than to assert the possession of them by the sword. Thus the practice of buying Indian titles is but the substitute which humanity and expediency have imposed, in place of the sword, in arriving at the actual enjoyment of property claimed by the right of discovery, and sanctioned by the natural superiority allowed to the claims of civilized communities over those of savage tribes. Up to the present time so invariable has been the operation of certain causes, first in diminishing the value of forest lands to the Indians, and secondly in disposing them to sell readily, that the plan of buying their right of occupancy has never threatened to retard, in any perceptible degree, the prosperity of any of the States.” (Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, No. 227, p. 6.)]

These are great evils, and I must add that they seem to me beyond remedy. I believe that the native nations of North America are doomed to perish, and that once the Europeans are established on the shores of the Pacific Ocean, that race of men will be no more. *i The Native Americans had only two alternatives, war or civilization. In other words, they had to either destroy the Europeans or become their equals.

i [ Almost all American statesmen seem, in fact, to hold this opinion. “Judging of the future by the past,” says Mr. Cass, “we cannot err in anticipating a progressive diminution of their numbers, and their eventual extinction, unless our border should become stationary, and they be removed beyond it, or unless some radical change should take place in the principles of our intercourse with them, which it is easier to hope for than to expect.”]

When the colonies were first settled, the Native Americans might have been able, by uniting their forces, to rid themselves of the small bodies of strangers landing on their continent. *j They tried several times and were on the point of succeeding. But today the disproportion between their resources and those of the whites is too great for such an undertaking to be considered. Nevertheless, from time to time men of penetration do arise among them who foresee the final destiny awaiting the native population and who strive to unite all the tribes in common hostility to the Europeans. Their efforts are in vain. The tribes near the whites are too weakened to offer effective resistance. The others give way to the childish carelessness about tomorrow that marks savage life, and wait until danger is close before preparing to meet it. Some are unable to make the effort, the others unwilling.

j [ Among other warlike enterprises was one by the Wampanaogs and other confederate tribes under Metacom in 1675 against the colonists of New England; the English were also engaged in war in Virginia in 1622.]
It is easy to foresee that the Native Americans will never adapt to civilization, or that it will be too late whenever they may be inclined to try.

Civilization is the result of a long social process that takes place in one spot and is handed down from one generation to the next, each profiting from the experience of the one before. Of all nations, those that live habitually by hunting submit to civilization with the most difficulty. Pastoral tribes, it is true, often change their place of abode, but they follow a regular order in their migrations and often return to their old stations, whereas the hunter’s dwelling changes with that of the animals he pursues.

Several attempts have been made to spread knowledge among the Native Americans without controlling their wandering tendencies, by the Jesuits in Canada and by the Puritans in New England. *k None of these efforts was crowned with any lasting success. Civilization began in the cabin, but it soon withdrew to die in the woods. The great error of these lawgivers to the Native Americans was that they did not understand that, to civilize a people, one must first make it settle, and this cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil. The Native Americans should first have been accustomed to agriculture. But not only do they lack this indispensable first step toward civilization, they would have great difficulty acquiring it. Men who have once given themselves up to the restless and adventurous life of the hunter feel an insurmountable disgust for the constant and regular labor that farming requires. We see this proved within our own society, but it is far more visible among peoples whose fondness for the chase is part of their national character.
k [ See the “Histoire de la Nouvelle France,” by Charlevoix, and the work entitled “Lettres edifiantes.”]

Apart from this general difficulty, there is another that applies especially to the Native Americans: they consider labor not merely an evil but a disgrace, so that their pride keeps them from becoming civilized as much as their indolence does. *l

l [ “In all the tribes,” says Volney, in his “Tableau des Etats-Unis,” p. 423, “there still exists a generation of old warriors, who cannot forbear, when they see their countrymen using the hoe, from exclaiming against the degradation of ancient manners, and asserting that the savages owe their decline to these innovations; adding, that they have only to return to their primitive habits in order to recover their power and their glory.”]

There is no Native American so wretched that he does not keep, under his hut of bark, a lofty idea of his personal worth. He considers the cares of industry and labor degrading occupations. He compares the farmer to the ox that draws the furrow, and even in our most ingenious handicrafts he sees nothing but the work of slaves. It is not that he lacks admiration for the power and intellectual greatness of the whites. But although the results of our efforts amaze him, he despises the means by which we achieve them, and while he acknowledges our ascendancy, he still believes in his own superiority. War and hunting are the only pursuits that seem to him worthy of a man. *m In the dreary solitude of his woods, the Native American cherishes the same ideas and opinions as the noble of the Middle Ages in his castle, and to complete the resemblance he needs only to become a conqueror. Thus, strange as it may seem, it is in the forests of the New World, and not among the Europeans who populate its coasts, that the ancient prejudices of Europe still survive.

m [ The following description appears in an official document: “Until a young man has been engaged with an enemy, and has performed some acts of valor, he gains no consideration, but is regarded nearly as a woman. In their great war-dances all the warriors in succession strike the post, as it is called, and recount their exploits. On these occasions their auditory consists of the kinsmen, friends, and comrades of the narrator. The profound impression which his discourse produces on them is manifested by the silent attention it receives, and by the loud shouts which hail its termination. The young man who finds himself at such a meeting without anything to recount is very unhappy; and instances have sometimes occurred of young warriors, whose passions had been thus inflamed, quitting the war-dance suddenly, and going off alone to seek for trophies which they might exhibit, and adventures which they might be allowed to relate.”]

More than once in the course of this work I have tried to explain the prodigious influence that social condition seems to have on the laws and customs of men, and I ask leave to add a few words on the same subject.

When I perceive the resemblance between the political institutions of our ancestors the Germans and those of the wandering tribes of North America, and between the customs described by Tacitus and those I have sometimes witnessed, I cannot help thinking that the same cause has produced the same results in both hemispheres. I think that amid the apparent diversity of human affairs, a certain number of primary facts can be discovered from which all the others derive. In what we usually call the German institutions, then, I am inclined to see only barbarian habits, and in what we call feudal principles, the opinions of savages.

However strongly the vices and prejudices of the Native Americans of North America may stand in the way of their becoming farmers and civilized, necessity sometimes forces them to it. Several of the Southern nations, among them the Cherokees and the Creeks, *n found themselves surrounded by Europeans. These Europeans had landed on the shores of the Atlantic, and, whether they came down the Ohio or up the Mississippi, they reached the tribes’ borders at the same time. These tribes have not been driven from place to place, as their Northern brethren were. Instead, they have been gradually hemmed into narrow limits, like game in a thicket before the hunters plunge into the interior. Placed between civilization and death, they found themselves obliged to live by degrading labor, like the whites. They took up agriculture, and, without entirely giving up their old habits and customs, they sacrificed only as much as was necessary to survive.

n [ These nations are now absorbed into the States of Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. The South once had four great nations (remnants of which still survive): the Choctaws, the Chickasaws, the Creeks, and the Cherokees. In 1830 the remnants of these four nations numbered about 75,000 individuals. It is estimated that about 300,000 Native Americans now remain in the territory occupied or claimed by the Anglo-American Union. (See Proceedings of the Indian Board in the City of New York.) The official documents supplied to Congress put the number at 313,130. A reader who wants to know the names and numerical strength of all the tribes living in Anglo-American territory should consult the documents I refer to. (Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, pp. 90–105.) [In the Census of 1870 it is stated that the Indian population of the United States is only 25,731, of whom 7,241 are in California.]]

The Cherokees went further. They created a written language and established a permanent form of government. And since everything moves fast in the New World, they set up a newspaper before they all had clothes. *o
o [ I brought back with me to France one or two copies of this unusual publication.]

The growth of European habits among these Native Americans has been remarkably speeded up by the mixed race that has arisen among them. *p Drawing its education from the father’s side, without entirely losing the savage customs of the mother, the person of mixed race forms the natural link between civilization and barbarism. Wherever this mixed race has multiplied, the savage state has been modified, and a great change has taken place in the customs of the people. *q

p [ See in the Report of the Committee on Indian Affairs, 21st Congress, No. 227, p. 23, why the number of people of mixed blood has grown among the Cherokees. The main cause goes back to the War of Independence. Many Anglo-Americans in Georgia had sided with England and had to flee to the Native Americans, among whom they married.]

q [ Unhappily the mixed race has been less numerous and less influential in North America than in any other country. The American continent was peopled by two great nations of Europe, the French and the English. The French were quick to form ties with the daughters of the natives. But there was an unfortunate affinity between the Native American character and their own. Instead of giving the savages the tastes and habits of civilized life, the French too often became passionately fond of the wild freedom they found them in. They became the most dangerous inhabitants of the wilderness, and won the friendship of the Native Americans by exaggerating both their vices and their virtues. M. de Senonville, the governor of Canada, wrote to Louis XIV in 1685: “It has long been believed that in order to civilize the savages we ought to draw them nearer to us. But there is every reason to suppose we have been mistaken. The Englishman, by contrast, stayed stubbornly attached to the customs and even the most trivial habits of his forefathers. He has remained in the midst of the American wilderness just what he was in the heart of European cities. He would allow no contact with savages whom he despised, and he carefully avoided any union of his race with theirs. Thus, while the French exercised no wholesome influence over the Native Americans, the English have always remained strangers to them.]

The success of the Cherokees proves that Native Americans are capable of civilization, but it does not prove that they will succeed in it. The difficulty they find in submitting to civilization comes from a general cause, which it is almost impossible for them to escape. A careful look at history shows that, in general, barbarous nations have raised themselves to civilization gradually, and by their own efforts. Whenever they have drawn knowledge from a foreign people, they have stood toward it as conquerors, not as a conquered nation. When the conquered nation is educated and the conquerors are half savage, as when the Northern nations invaded Rome or the Mongols invaded China, the power that victory gives the barbarian is enough to keep up his importance among civilized men and to let him rank as their equal until he becomes their rival. The one has might on his side, the other has intelligence; the former admires the knowledge and the arts of the conquered, and the latter envies the power of the conquerors. The barbarians at length admit civilized man into their palaces, and he in turn opens his schools to the barbarians. But when the side that holds the physical force also holds the intellectual advantage, the conquered party seldom becomes civilized: it retreats, or is destroyed. It may therefore be said, in a general way, that savages go out in arms to seek knowledge, but that they do not accept it when it comes to them.

If the Native American tribes that now live in the heart of the continent could summon up enough energy to try to civilize themselves, they might possibly succeed. Already superior to the barbarous nations around them, they would gradually gain strength and experience. When the Europeans appeared on their borders, they would be in a position, if not to maintain their independence, at least to assert their right to the soil and to merge with the conquerors. But the misfortune of the Native Americans is that they have come into contact with a civilized people that is also (it must be admitted) the most avaricious nation on the globe, while they are still semi-barbarous. They find despots in their teachers, and they receive knowledge from the hand of oppression. Living in the freedom of the woods, the Native American of North America was poor, but he felt inferior to no one. As soon as he wants to enter the social scale of the whites, however, he takes the lowest rank in society, for he enters the circle of science and wealth ignorant and poor. He has led a life of agitation, beset with evils and dangers but filled at the same time with proud emotions. *r Now he is obliged to submit to a wearisome, obscure, and degraded state, and to earn the bread that feeds him by hard and ignoble labor. In his eyes these are the only results civilization can boast of, and even this much he is not sure to obtain.

r [ The adventurous life of the hunter has a certain irresistible charm, which seizes the heart of man and carries him away in spite of reason and experience. The memoirs of Tanner show this plainly. Tanner is a European who was carried off by Native Americans at the age of six and remained with them in the woods for thirty years. Nothing can be imagined more appalling than the miseries he describes. He tells us of tribes without a chief, families without a nation to call their own, men in a state of isolation, and the wrecks of powerful tribes wandering at random amid the ice and snow and desolate solitudes of Canada. When Native Americans try to imitate their European neighbors and to till the earth as the settlers do, they are immediately exposed to very formidable competition. The white man is skilled in the craft of agriculture; the Native American is a rough beginner in an art he does not know. The white man reaps abundant crops without difficulty, while the Native American meets a thousand obstacles in raising the fruits of the earth.

The European lives among a population whose wants he knows and shares. The savage is isolated in the midst of a hostile people, with whose customs, language, and laws he is imperfectly acquainted, but without whose help he cannot live. He can obtain the means of comfort only by bartering his goods for the goods of the European, since the help of his own countrymen is wholly insufficient to meet his wants. When the Native American wants to sell the produce of his labor, he cannot always find a buyer, while the European readily finds a market. And the former can produce only at considerable cost what the latter sells at a very low price. Thus the Native American has no sooner escaped the evils to which barbarous nations are exposed than he is subjected to the still greater miseries of civilized communities. He finds it scarcely less difficult to live in the midst of our abundance than in the depths of his own wilderness.

He has not yet lost the habits of his wandering life; the traditions of his fathers and his passion for the chase are still alive within him. The wild pleasures that once animated him in the woods painfully excite his troubled imagination, and his former hardships seem less harsh to him, his former dangers less appalling. He contrasts the independence he enjoyed among his equals with the servile position he holds in civilized society. On the other hand, the wilderness that was so long his free home is still close at hand; a few hours’ march will bring him back to it. The whites offer him a sum, which seems considerable to him, for the ground he has begun to clear. This money from the Europeans may possibly give him the means of a happy and peaceful living in remoter regions. So he leaves the plow, takes up his native weapons again, and returns to the wilderness forever. *s The condition of the Creeks and Cherokees, to which I have already alluded, fully confirms the truth of this sad picture.

In the last few years the Anglo-Americans have moved into this province, which is still thinly peopled. If the different degrees of European civilization, which differ comparatively little, produce results of such magnitude, we can readily imagine the consequences that must follow when the most advanced European civilization collides with Native American savages.]

In the little they have done, the Native Americans have unquestionably shown as much natural genius as the peoples of Europe in their most important undertakings. But nations, like individuals, need time to learn, whatever their intelligence and zeal. While the savages were engaged in the work of civilization, the Europeans kept surrounding them on every side and confining them within narrower limits. The two races gradually met, and they now stand in immediate juxtaposition. The Native American is already superior to his barbarous parent, but he is still very far below his white neighbor. With their resources and acquired knowledge, the Europeans soon took for themselves most of the advantages the natives might have drawn from owning the soil. They have settled in the country; they have bought land at a very low price or occupied it by force; and the Native Americans have been ruined by a competition they had no means of resisting. They were isolated in their own country, and their race was only a colony of troublesome aliens in the midst of a numerous and domineering people. *t

t [ See in the Legislative Documents (21st Congress, No. 89) instances of every kind of excess committed by the whites on the territory of the Native Americans. The whites took possession of part of their lands until the troops of Congress forced them to withdraw, or they carried off their cattle, burned their houses, cut down their corn, and did violence to their persons. It appears nevertheless from all these documents that the claims of the natives are constantly protected by the government against the abuse of force. The Union has a representative agent continually employed to reside among the Native Americans, and the report of the Cherokee agent, which is among the documents I have referred to, is almost always favorable to them. “The intrusion of whites,” he says, “upon the lands of the Cherokees would cause ruin to the poor, helpless, and inoffensive inhabitants.” And he further remarks, about the attempt of the State of Georgia to establish a division line limiting the boundaries of the Cherokees, that the line drawn, having been made by the whites and entirely upon ex parte evidence of their several rights, was of no validity whatever.]

Washington said in one of his messages to Congress, “We are more enlightened and more powerful than the Indian nations, we are therefore bound in honor to treat them with kindness and even with generosity.” That virtuous and high-minded policy has not been followed. The settlers’ greed is usually backed by the tyranny of the government. The Cherokees and the Creeks are established on the territory they inhabited before the Europeans settled, and the Americans have often treated with them as with foreign nations. Even so, the surrounding States have not agreed to recognize them as independent peoples, and attempts have been made to subject these children of the woods to Anglo-American magistrates, laws, and customs. *u Destitution had driven these unfortunate people to civilization, and oppression now drives them back to their former condition. Many of them abandon the soil they had begun to clear and return to their savage way of life.
u [ In 1829 the State of Alabama split the Creek territory into counties and placed the Native American population under the authority of European magistrates.

When these laws were enforced upon the Choctaws, who lived in that district, the tribe assembled. Their chief told them what the whites intended and read them some of the laws they were meant to submit to. They unanimously declared that it was better to retreat into the wilds again at once.]
Chapter XVIII: Future Condition of Three Races — Part III

If we consider the tyrannical measures adopted by the legislatures of the Southern States, the conduct of their Governors, and the decrees of their courts of justice, we shall be convinced that the final aim of their policy is the complete expulsion of the Native Americans. The Americans of that part of the Union look on the aborigines with jealousy. *v They know that these tribes have not yet lost the traditions of savage life, and before civilization has fixed them permanently to the soil, they intend to force them to withdraw by driving them to despair. The Creeks and Cherokees, oppressed by the several States, have appealed to the central government. It is by no means indifferent to their misfortunes and sincerely wants to save the remnant of the natives and keep them in free possession of the territory that the Union is pledged to respect. *w But the several States offer such formidable resistance to carrying out this plan that the government is obliged to consent to the destruction of a few barbarous tribes, so as not to endanger the safety of the American Union.

v [ The Georgians, who are so troubled by having Native Americans nearby, live in a territory that at present has no more than seven inhabitants to the square mile. In France the same area holds one hundred and sixty-two inhabitants.]

w [ In 1818 Congress appointed commissioners to visit the Arkansas Territory, accompanied by a deputation of Creeks, Choctaws, and Chickasaws. This expedition was commanded by Messrs. Kennerly, M’Coy, Wash Hood, and John Bell. See the different reports of the commissioners, and their journal, in the Documents of Congress, No. 87, House of Representatives.]

But the federal government, which cannot protect the Native Americans, would gladly ease the hardships of their lot. With this intention, proposals have been made to transport them at public expense to more remote regions.

Between the thirty-third and thirty-seventh degrees of north latitude lies a vast tract of country, which has taken the name of Arkansas from the principal river that waters it. It is bounded on one side by the borders of Mexico and on the other by the Mississippi. Numberless streams cross it in every direction; the climate is mild and the soil productive, but only a few wandering hordes of savages live there. The government of the Union wants to transport the broken remnants of the indigenous population of the South to the part of this country nearest Mexico and at a great distance from the American settlements.

We were assured, toward the end of the year 1831, that 10,000 Native Americans had already gone down to the shores of the Arkansas, and fresh detachments were constantly following them. But Congress has been unable to arouse a unanimous determination in those it wants to protect. Some, indeed, are willing to leave the seat of oppression, but the most educated members of the community refuse to abandon their new homes and their growing crops. They believe that the work of civilization, once interrupted, will never be resumed. They fear that the domestic habits they have so recently acquired may be irretrievably lost in a country that is still barbarous, where nothing is prepared for the support of an agricultural people. They know that hostile hordes will oppose their entry into those wilds, and that they have lost the energy of barbarians without gaining the resources of civilization to resist their attacks. Moreover, they readily see that the settlement proposed to them is merely a temporary expedient. Who can assure them that they will at length be allowed to live in peace in their new retreat? The United States pledges itself to keep its obligation, but the territory they now occupy was formerly secured to them by the most solemn oaths of Anglo-American good faith. *x The American government does not indeed rob them of their lands, but it allows constant incursions upon them. In a few years the same white population that now crowds around them will track them to the solitudes of the Arkansas. They will then be exposed to the same evils without the same remedies, and since the limits of the earth will at last fail them, their only refuge is the grave.

x [ The fifth article of the treaty made with the Creeks in August, 1790, reads as follows: — “The United States solemnly guarantee to the Creek nation all their land within the limits of the United States.”

The seventh article of the treaty concluded in 1791 with the Cherokees says: — “The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee nation all their lands not hereby ceded.” The next article declared that if any citizen of the United States, or any other settler not of the Indian race, should settle on Cherokee territory, the United States would withdraw its protection from that person and hand him over to be punished as the Cherokee nation saw fit.]

The Union treats the Native Americans with less greed and harshness than the policy of the several States does, but the two governments are equally lacking in good faith. The States extend to the tribes what they are pleased to call the benefits of their laws, believing that the tribes will withdraw rather than submit. And the central government, which promises these unhappy people a permanent refuge, is well aware that it cannot secure it to them. *y

y [ That does not stop them from promising it in the most solemn manner. See the letter of the President addressed to the Creek Indians, March 23, 1829 (Proceedings of the Indian Board, in the city of New York, p. 5): “Beyond the great river Mississippi, where a part of your nation has gone, your father has provided a country large enough for all of you, and he advises you to remove to it. There your white brothers will not trouble you; they will have no claim to the land, and you can live upon it, you and all your children, as long as the grass grows, or the water runs, in peace and plenty. It will be yours forever.”

The Secretary of War, in a letter written to the Cherokees on April 18, 1829 (see the same work, p. 6), tells them that they cannot expect to keep possession of the lands they then occupied. But he gives them the most positive assurance of uninterrupted peace if they will move beyond the Mississippi. It is as if the power that could not protect them then would be able to protect them later!]

Thus the tyranny of the States forces the savages to retire, and the Union, by its promises and resources, makes their retreat easier. These measures tend to precisely the same end. *z “By the will of our Father in Heaven, the Governor of the whole world,” said the Cherokees in their petition to Congress, *a “the red man of America has become small, and the white man great and renowned. When the ancestors of the people of these United States first came to the shores of America they found the red man strong: though he was ignorant and savage, yet he received them kindly, and gave them dry land to rest their weary feet. They met in peace, and shook hands in token of friendship. Whatever the white man wanted and asked of the Indian, the latter willingly gave. At that time the Indian was the lord, and the white man the suppliant. But now the scene has changed. The strength of the red man has become weakness. As his neighbors increased in numbers his power became less and less, and now, of the many and powerful tribes who once covered these United States, only a few are to be seen — a few whom a sweeping pestilence has left. The northern tribes, who were once so numerous and powerful, are now nearly extinct. Thus it has happened to the red man of America. Shall we, who are remnants, share the same fate?”

“The land on which we stand we have received as an inheritance from our fathers, who possessed it from time immemorial, as a gift from our common Father in Heaven. They bequeathed it to us as their children, and we have sacredly kept it, as containing the remains of our beloved men. This right of inheritance we have never ceded nor ever forfeited. Permit us to ask what better right can the people have to a country than the right of inheritance and immemorial peaceable possession? We know it is said of late by the State of Georgia and by the Executive of the United States, that we have forfeited this right; but we think this is said gratuitously. At what time have we made the forfeit? What great crime have we committed, whereby we must forever be divested of our country and rights? Was it when we were hostile to the United States, and took part with the King of Great Britain, during the struggle for independence? If so, why was not this forfeiture declared in the first treaty of peace between the United States and our beloved men? Why was not such an article as the following inserted in the treaty: — ‘The United States give peace to the Cherokees, but, for the part they took in the late war, declare them to be but tenants at will, to be removed when the convenience of the States, within whose chartered limits they live, shall require it’? That was the proper time to assume such a possession. But it was not thought of, nor would our forefathers have agreed to any treaty whose tendency was to deprive them of their rights and their country.”

Such is the language of the Native Americans. Their assertions are true and their forebodings unavoidable. From whichever side we consider the destiny of the aborigines of North America, their calamities appear beyond remedy. If they remain barbarous, they are forced to retire. If they try to civilize their customs, contact with a more civilized community subjects them to oppression and destitution. They perish if they keep wandering from waste to waste, and if they try to settle, they must still perish. The help of Europeans is necessary to teach them, but the approach of Europeans corrupts them and drives them back into savage life. They refuse to change their habits as long as their wilderness is their own, and it is too late to change them when they are forced to submit.

The Spaniards hunted the Native Americans with bloodhounds, like wild beasts. They sacked the New World with no more restraint or compassion than a city taken by storm. But destruction must cease and frenzy must end. The remnant of the Native American population that had escaped the massacre mixed with its conquerors and in the end adopted their religion and their customs. *b The conduct of the Americans of the United States toward the aborigines, on the other hand, is marked by a singular attachment to the formalities of law. As long as the Native Americans remain in their barbarous condition, the Americans take no part in their affairs. They treat them as independent nations, and they do not take possession of their hunting grounds without a treaty of purchase. And if a Native American nation happens to be so encroached upon that it cannot live on its territory, they give it brotherly help in transporting it to a grave far enough away from the land of its fathers.

b [ The honor of this result, however, is by no means due to the Spaniards. If the Native American tribes had not been tillers of the ground when the Europeans arrived, they would unquestionably have been destroyed in South America as well as in North America.]

The Spaniards could not wipe out the Native American race, even by those unparalleled atrocities that brand them with lasting shame, nor did they entirely succeed in stripping it of its rights. The Americans of the United States have achieved both aims with remarkable ease: quietly, legally, philanthropically, without shedding blood, and without breaking a single great principle of morality in the eyes of the world. *c It is impossible to destroy men with more respect for the laws of humanity.

The more I think about how civilized and uncivilized man differ in their approach to the principles of justice, the more I see that the former disputes the justice of the very rights that the latter simply violates.]

Situation of the Black Population in the United States, and Dangers with Which Its Presence Threatens the Whites

The Native Americans will perish in the same isolation in which they have lived. But the destiny of Black people is to some extent interwoven with that of the Europeans. These two races are attached to each other without intermingling, and they are equally unable either to separate entirely or to combine. The most formidable of all the ills that threaten the future existence of the Union comes from the presence of a Black population on its territory. When the observer looks for the cause of the present embarrassments or the future dangers of the United States, he is invariably led to this as a primary fact.

The lasting evils that afflict mankind are usually produced by the violent or growing efforts of men. But there is one calamity that crept stealthily into the world and was at first scarcely distinguishable amid the ordinary abuses of power. It began with an individual whose name history has not preserved. It was carried like some accursed seed to one portion of the soil, but afterward it fed itself, grew without effort, and spreads naturally with the society to which it belongs. I need hardly add that this calamity is slavery. Christianity suppressed slavery, but the Christians of the sixteenth century reestablished it, as an exception, indeed, to their social system, and restricted to one of the races of mankind. Yet the wound thus inflicted on humanity, though less extensive, was at the same time made far harder to cure.

It is important to distinguish accurately between slavery itself and its consequences. The immediate evils produced by slavery were very nearly the same in antiquity as they are among the moderns, but the consequences of these evils were different. Among the ancients, the slave belonged to the same race as his master and was often the superior of the two in education *d and learning. Freedom was the only distinction between them, and when freedom was granted they were easily blended together. The ancients, then, had a very simple means of avoiding slavery and its evil consequences, which was emancipation; and they succeeded as soon as they adopted this measure generally. This is not to say that in ancient States no traces of servitude lingered for some time after servitude itself was abolished. There is a natural prejudice that leads men to despise anyone who was once their inferior long after he has become their equal. The real inequality produced by fortune or by law is always followed by an imaginary inequality planted in the customs of the people. Nevertheless, among the ancients this secondary consequence of slavery lasted only a limited time, for the freedman so completely resembled those born free that it soon became impossible to tell him apart from them.

d [ It is well known that several of the most distinguished authors of antiquity, among them Aesop and Terence, were or had been slaves. Slaves were not always taken from barbarous nations; the fortunes of war also reduced highly civilized men to servitude.]

The greatest difficulty in antiquity was changing the law; among the moderns it is changing the customs. And as far as we are concerned, the real obstacles begin where those of the ancients ended. This comes from the fact that, among the moderns, the abstract and transient fact of slavery is fatally joined to the physical and permanent fact of color. The tradition of slavery dishonors the race, and the distinctiveness of the race keeps the tradition of slavery alive. No African has ever voluntarily emigrated to the shores of the New World, and from this it must be inferred that all the Black people now found in that hemisphere are either slaves or freedmen. Thus the Black person passes the eternal mark of his disgrace on to all his descendants, and although the law may abolish slavery, God alone can erase the traces of its existence.

The modern slave differs from his master not only in his condition but in his origin. You can set a Black person free, but you cannot make him anything other than a foreigner to the European. Nor is this all. We scarcely recognize the common features of humanity in this child of degradation whom slavery has brought among us. His face seems hideous to us, his understanding weak, his tastes low; and we are almost inclined to regard him as a being halfway between man and the brutes. *e Thus, once the moderns have abolished slavery, they have three prejudices to fight, which are harder to attack and far harder to overcome than the mere fact of servitude: the prejudice of the master, the prejudice of race, and the prejudice of color.

e [ For the whites to give up the opinion they have formed of the moral and intellectual inferiority of their former slaves, Black people would have to change; but as long as that opinion lasts, change is impossible.]

It is hard for us, who have been fortunate enough to be born among men who are like us by nature and equal to us by law, to grasp the irreconcilable differences that separate Black Americans from Europeans in America. But we can form a faint idea of them by analogy. France was once a country with many distinctions of rank that had been created by legislation. Nothing is more artificial than a purely legal inferiority; nothing is more contrary to the instinct of mankind than these permanent divisions set up between beings who are plainly alike. Yet these divisions lasted for ages; in many places they still last; and everywhere they have left imaginary traces that only time can wear away. If it is so hard to root out an inequality that originates solely in the law, how can we destroy distinctions that seem to rest on the unchangeable laws of Nature herself? When I recall how extremely difficult it is for aristocratic bodies, of whatever kind, to blend with the mass of the people, and how very carefully they guard the ideal boundaries of their caste, I despair of seeing an aristocracy disappear when it is founded on visible and indelible signs. Those who hope that Europeans will ever mix with Black people seem to me to deceive themselves; neither my own reason nor the evidence of facts leads me to any such conclusion.

Until now, wherever the whites have been the most powerful, they have kept Black people in a subordinate or servile position; wherever Black people have been strongest, they have destroyed the whites. That is the only retribution that has ever taken place between the two races.

I see that in one part of the territory of the United States today, the legal barrier between the two races is tending to fall away, but not the barrier that exists in the customs of the country. Slavery recedes, but the prejudice it gave birth to stays where it was. Anyone who has lived in the United States must have noticed that in the parts of the Union where Black people are no longer slaves, they have in no way drawn closer to the whites. On the contrary, race prejudice appears stronger in the States that have abolished slavery than in those where it still exists; and nowhere is it so intolerant as in the States where servitude has never been known.

It is true that in the North of the Union marriages between Black people and whites may be legally contracted; but public opinion would condemn as infamous a man who married a Black woman, and it would be hard to find a single instance of such a union. The right to vote has been granted to Black people in almost all the States that have abolished slavery; but if they come forward to vote, their lives are in danger. If they are wronged, they may bring a lawsuit, but they will find only whites among their judges; and although they may legally serve as jurors, prejudice drives them away from that duty. The same schools do not admit the Black child and the European child. In the theaters, no amount of gold can buy a seat for the servile race beside their former masters; in the hospitals they lie apart; and although they are allowed to call on the same God as the whites, it must be at a different altar, in their own churches, with their own clergy. The gates of Heaven are not closed against these unhappy people; but their inferiority follows them to the very edge of the other world. When a Black man dies, his bones are cast aside, and the distinction of condition prevails even in the equality of death. The Black man is free, but he can share neither the rights, nor the pleasures, nor the labor, nor the sorrows, nor the tomb of the man whose equal he has been declared to be; and he cannot meet him on fair terms in life or in death.

In the South, where slavery still exists, Black people are kept apart less carefully. They sometimes share the labor and the recreations of the whites; the whites agree to mix with them to a certain extent; and although the legislation treats them more harshly, the habits of the people are more tolerant and compassionate. In the South the master is not afraid to raise his slave to his own level, because he knows he can reduce him to the dust in a moment whenever he pleases. In the North the white man no longer sees clearly the barrier that separates him from the degraded race, and he avoids Black people all the more stubbornly because he fears that one day they might be confused with him.

Among the Americans of the South, nature sometimes claims her rights again and brings back a fleeting equality between Black people and whites; in the North, though, pride holds in check the most commanding of human passions. The American of the Northern States would perhaps allow a Black woman to share his licentious pleasures, if the laws of his country did not declare that she may aspire to be the lawful partner of his bed; but he recoils in horror from the woman who might become his wife.

Thus it is that in the United States the prejudice that repels Black people seems to grow in proportion as they are emancipated, and inequality is sanctioned by the customs of the country while it is erased from its laws. But if the relative position of the two races living in the United States is what I have described, it may be asked why the Americans have abolished slavery in the North of the Union, why they maintain it in the South, and why they make its hardships worse there. The answer is easily given. It is not for the good of Black people but for that of the whites that measures are taken to abolish slavery in the United States.

The first Black people were brought into Virginia about the year 1621. *f In America, therefore, as in the rest of the world, slavery began in the South. From there it spread from one settlement to another; but the number of slaves fell off toward the Northern States, and the Black population was always very small in New England. *g

f [ See Beverley’s “History of Virginia.” See also, in Jefferson’s “Memoirs,” some interesting details about how Black people were first brought into Virginia, and about the first Act, passed in 1778, that prohibited their importation.]

g [ The number of slaves was smaller in the North, but the advantages that came from slavery were no more disputed there than in the South.
