Scarcely a century had passed since the founding of the colonies when the planters were struck by an extraordinary fact: the provinces with comparatively few slaves grew in population, wealth, and prosperity more rapidly than those with the greatest number of Black people. In the former, it is true, the inhabitants had to cultivate the soil themselves or by hired laborers; in the latter they were supplied with hands for which they paid no wages. Yet although labor and expense were on one side, and ease with economy on the other, the former provinces had the more advantageous system. This result seemed all the harder to explain because the settlers all belonged to the same European race, and had the same habits, the same civilization, and the same laws, and their differences were extremely slight.

Time went on, however, and the Anglo-Americans spread beyond the coasts of the Atlantic Ocean and pushed farther and farther into the wilderness of the West. They met with new soil and an unfamiliar climate; the obstacles in their way were of the most varied kind; their races intermingled; the inhabitants of the South went north, and those of the North went south. But amid all these causes, the same result appeared at every step, and in general the colonies without slaves became more populous and richer than those where slavery flourished. The further progress went, the more it was shown that slavery, so cruel to the slave, is harmful to the master.

But this truth was demonstrated most fully when civilization reached the banks of the Ohio. The river that the Native Americans called Ohio, or Beautiful River, waters one of the most magnificent valleys ever made the home of man. Rolling land stretches along both shores of the Ohio, and its soil offers inexhaustible treasures to the farmer. On either bank the air is healthy and the climate mild, and each bank forms the far frontier of a vast State. The one that follows the many windings of the Ohio on the left is called Kentucky; the one on the right bears the name of the river. These two States differ in only one respect: Kentucky has admitted slavery, but the State of Ohio has forbidden slaves within its borders. *h
h [ Not only is slavery prohibited in Ohio, but no free Black people are allowed to enter the territory of that State, or to hold property in it. See the Statutes of Ohio.]

Thus the traveler who floats down the Ohio to the place where it flows into the Mississippi may be said to sail between liberty and servitude; and a quick look at the surrounding scene will convince him which of the two is more favorable to mankind. On the left bank the population is sparse; from time to time one sees a band of slaves loitering in the half-deserted fields; the primeval forest returns at every turn; society seems asleep and man idle, and nature alone offers a scene of activity and life. From the right bank, by contrast, a confused hum is heard that announces the presence of industry; the fields are covered with abundant harvests; the elegance of the dwellings shows the taste and activity of the farmer; and man appears to enjoy the wealth and contentment that are the reward of labor. *i

i [ Ohio’s energy is not limited to individuals; the State’s own undertakings are remarkably large. A canal now links Lake Erie to the Ohio, so that the valley of the Mississippi is connected with the river of the North, and European goods landed at New York can travel by water all the way to New Orleans, across five hundred leagues of continent.]

The State of Kentucky was founded in 1775, the State of Ohio only twelve years later; but twelve years count for more in America than half a century in Europe, and today the population of Ohio exceeds that of Kentucky by two hundred and fifty thousand souls. *j These opposite consequences of slavery and freedom are easy to understand, and they are enough to explain many of the differences we see between the civilization of antiquity and that of our own time.
j [ The exact numbers given by the census of 1830 were: Kentucky, 688,-844; Ohio, 937,679. [In 1890 the population of Ohio was 3,672,316, that of Kentucky, 1,858,635.]]

On the left bank of the Ohio, labor is associated with the idea of slavery; on the right bank, it is identified with prosperity and improvement. On the one side it is degraded, on the other it is honored. In the former territory no white laborers can be found, for they would be afraid of being assimilated to Black people; in the latter no one is idle, for the white population brings its activity and its intelligence to every kind of employment. Thus the men whose task is to cultivate the rich soil of Kentucky are ignorant and lukewarm, while those who are active and educated either do nothing or move over to the State of Ohio, where they can work without dishonor.

It is true that in Kentucky the planters do not have to pay wages to the slaves they employ; but they get small profits from their labor, whereas the wages paid to free workmen would come back with interest in the value of their services. The free workman is paid, but he does his work faster than the slave, and speed of execution is one of the great elements of economy. The white man sells his services, but they are bought only when they happen to be useful; the Black man can claim no payment for his toil, but the cost of his upkeep never stops. He must be supported in his old age as well as in the prime of manhood, in his unprofitable childhood as well as in the productive years of youth. Payment must be made equally to obtain the services of either class of men: the free workman receives his wages in money, the slave in education, food, care, and clothing. The money a master spends on the upkeep of his slaves goes out gradually and in small amounts, so that it is scarcely noticed; the free workman’s wage is paid in a lump sum, which seems only to enrich the person who receives it. But in the end the slave has cost more than the free servant, and his labor is less productive. *k

k [ Apart from these causes, which make free labor more productive and more economical than slave labor wherever free workmen are plentiful, another cause can be pointed out that is particular to the United States: the sugar cane has until now been cultivated successfully only on the banks of the Mississippi, near the mouth of that river in the Gulf of Mexico. In Louisiana the cultivation of sugar cane is extremely profitable, and nowhere does a laborer earn so much by his work; and since there is always a certain relation between the cost of production and the value of the produce, the price of slaves is very high in Louisiana. But Louisiana is one of the confederated States, and slaves may be carried there from all parts of the Union; the price paid for slaves in New Orleans therefore raises the value of slaves in all the other markets. The consequence is that in the countries where the land is less productive, the cost of slave labor is still very considerable, which gives free labor an additional advantage in competition.]

The influence of slavery goes further still: it affects the character of the master and gives a particular bent to his ideas and tastes. On both banks of the Ohio the inhabitants are enterprising and energetic, but this vigor is used very differently in the two States. The white inhabitant of Ohio, who has to live by his own efforts, regards material prosperity as the main aim of his existence. The country he lives in offers inexhaustible resources to his industry and ever-changing temptations to his activity, so his eagerness to acquire goes beyond the ordinary limits of human greed. He is tormented by the desire for wealth, and he boldly takes every path that fortune opens to him. He becomes a sailor, a pioneer, an artisan, or a laborer with equal indifference, and he endures with equal constancy the hardships and dangers of these various professions. The resources of his intelligence are astonishing, and his eagerness in pursuit of gain amounts to a kind of heroism.

But the Kentuckian scorns not only labor but all the undertakings that labor promotes. Because he lives in idle independence, his tastes are those of an idle man; money loses part of its value in his eyes; he covets wealth much less than pleasure and excitement; and the energy his neighbor devotes to making money turns, in him, into a passionate love of field sports and military exercises. He delights in violent bodily exertion, he is familiar with the use of arms, and from a very early age he is accustomed to risk his life in single combat. Thus slavery not only keeps the whites from becoming wealthy, it keeps them even from wishing to be.

The same causes have been producing opposite effects continually for the last two centuries in the British colonies of North America, and they have established a very striking difference between the commercial capacity of the inhabitants of the South and that of the North. Today only the Northern States possess shipping, manufactures, railroads, and canals. This difference can be seen not only in comparing the North with the South but also in comparing the several Southern States. Almost all the individuals who carry on commercial operations, or who try to turn slave labor to account, in the most southern districts of the Union have emigrated from the North. The natives of the Northern States are constantly spreading over the part of American territory where they have less competition to fear. They discover resources there that escaped the notice of the inhabitants; and since they go along with a system they do not approve of, they succeed in turning it to better advantage than the people who first founded it and still maintain it.

If I wished to continue this comparison, I could easily prove that almost all the differences we notice between the characters of the Americans in the Southern and the Northern States have originated in slavery; but that would take me away from my subject, and my present intention is to point out not all the consequences of servitude but only the effects it has had on the prosperity of the countries that have admitted it.

The influence of slavery on the production of wealth must have been understood very imperfectly in antiquity, since slavery then prevailed throughout the civilized world, and the nations that did not have it were barbarous. And indeed Christianity abolished slavery only by pleading the cause of the slave; at the present time it can be attacked in the name of the master, and on this point self-interest is reconciled with morality.

As these truths became plain in the United States, slavery gave way before the progress of experience. Servitude had begun in the South and had spread from there toward the North; but now it is retreating again. Freedom, which started from the North, now moves steadily down toward the South. Among the large States, Pennsylvania now forms the northern limit of slavery; but even within those limits the slave system is shaken. Maryland, which lies immediately below Pennsylvania, is preparing for its abolition; and Virginia, which comes next to Maryland, is already debating its usefulness and its dangers. *l

l [ One particular reason helps turn the last two States away from the cause of slavery. This part of the Union used to draw its wealth mainly from growing tobacco. That crop is grown especially by slaves; but in the last few years the market price of tobacco has dropped, while the value of slaves has stayed the same. So the ratio between the cost of production and the value of the produce has shifted. The people of Maryland and Virginia are therefore more willing than they were thirty years ago to give up slave labor in tobacco growing, or to give up slavery and tobacco together.]

No great change takes place in human institutions without the law of inheritance being among its causes. When the law of primogeniture prevailed in the South, each family was represented by one wealthy individual, who was neither forced nor encouraged to work. He was surrounded, like a tree by parasitic plants, by the other members of his family, who were then excluded by law from sharing the common inheritance and who lived the same kind of life as he did. The very same thing happened then in all the families of the South as still happens in the wealthy families of some European countries: the younger sons remain in the same state of idleness as their elder brother, without being as rich as he is. This identical result seems to be produced in Europe and in America by wholly similar causes. In the South of the United States the whole white race formed an aristocratic body, headed by a certain number of privileged individuals whose wealth was permanent and whose leisure was hereditary. These leaders of the American nobility kept alive the traditional prejudices of the white race, whose representatives they were, and upheld the honor of an inactive life. This aristocracy contained many who were poor, but none who would work; its members preferred want to labor. Consequently no competition arose against Black laborers and slaves, and whatever opinion might be held about the usefulness of their efforts, it was necessary to employ them, since there was no one else to work.

As soon as the law of primogeniture was abolished, fortunes began to shrink, and all the families of the country were reduced at the same time to a state in which labor became necessary to earn a living. Several of them have since disappeared entirely, and all of them learned to look ahead to the time when everyone would have to provide for his own needs. Wealthy individuals can still be found, but they no longer form a close-knit, hereditary body, nor have they been able to adopt a line of conduct that they could keep up and spread through all ranks of society. The prejudice that stigmatized labor was first abandoned by common consent; the number of needy men increased; and the needy were allowed to earn a hard living without blushing for their efforts. Thus one of the most immediate consequences of the division of estates has been to create a class of free laborers. As soon as competition began between the free laborer and the slave, the slave’s inferiority became obvious, and slavery was attacked at its fundamental principle, which is the interest of the master.

As slavery recedes, the Black population follows its backward course and returns with it toward the tropical regions from which it originally came. However odd this fact may seem at first, it is easily explained. Although the Americans abolish the principle of slavery, they do not set their slaves free. To illustrate this remark, I will take the example of the State of New York. In 1788 the State of New York prohibited the sale of slaves within its limits, which was an indirect way of prohibiting the importation of Black people. From then on the number of Black people could increase only at the rate of natural population growth. But eight years later a more decisive measure was taken, and it was enacted that all children born of slave parents after July 4, 1799, should be free. No increase could then take place; and although slaves still existed, slavery could be said to be abolished.

Once a Northern State prohibited the importation of slaves, no more slaves were brought from the South to be sold in its markets. On the other hand, because the sale of slaves was forbidden in that State, an owner could no longer rid himself of a slave who had become a burden, except by taking him to the South. And when a Northern State declared that a slave’s son should be born free, the slave lost a large share of his market value, since his descendants were no longer part of the bargain; the owner then had a strong interest in taking him to the South. Thus the same law keeps the slaves of the South from coming to the Northern States, and drives those of the North to the South.

A State feels the lack of free hands more as its slaves become fewer. But the more the work is done by free hands, the less productive slave labor becomes; the slave is then a useless or burdensome possession, and it is important to send him off to those Southern States where the same competition is not to be feared. Thus the abolition of slavery does not set the slave free: it merely transfers him from one master to another, and from the North to the South.

The emancipated Black people, and those born after the abolition of slavery, do not, indeed, move from the North to the South; but their situation in relation to the Europeans is not unlike that of the native peoples of America. They remain half civilized and deprived of their rights in the midst of a population far superior to them in wealth and in knowledge, where they are exposed to the tyranny of the laws *m and the intolerance of the people. In some respects they are even more to be pitied than the Native Americans, since they are haunted by the memory of slavery and cannot claim possession of a single piece of the soil. Many of them perish miserably, *n and the rest crowd into the large towns, where they do the lowest jobs and lead a wretched and precarious existence.

m [ States that have abolished slavery usually do whatever they can to make their territory an unpleasant place for Black people to live; and since the different States rival one another in this, these unhappy people can only choose the least of the evils surrounding them.]

n [ Death rates differ greatly between Black people and whites in the States that have abolished slavery. From 1820 to 1831 only one out of forty-two individuals of the white population died in Philadelphia, but one Black person out of twenty-one individuals of the Black population died in the same period. Among Black people who are still slaves, mortality is by no means so high. (See Emerson’s “Medical Statistics,” p. 28.)]

But even if the number of Black people continued to increase as fast as when they were still in slavery, the number of whites has grown twice as fast since the abolition of slavery, so Black people would soon be, as it were, lost in the midst of a foreign population.

A district cultivated by slaves is generally more thinly populated than a district cultivated by free labor. Moreover, America is still a new country, and a State is therefore not half populated when it abolishes slavery. As soon as slavery is ended, the lack of free labor is felt, and a crowd of enterprising adventurers arrives at once from all parts of the country, hurrying to profit from the fresh resources then opened to industry. The soil is soon divided among them, and a family of white settlers takes possession of each tract of land. Besides, European emigration goes exclusively to the free States; for what would be the fate of a poor emigrant who crosses the Atlantic in search of comfort and happiness if he landed in a country where labor is stigmatized as degrading?

Thus the white population grows by natural increase and, at the same time, by the immense influx of emigrants, while the Black population receives no emigrants and is declining. The proportion between the two races is soon reversed. Black people become a small remnant, a poor tribe of wanderers, lost in the midst of an immense people in full possession of the land; and their presence is marked only by the injustice and hardships of which they are the unhappy victims.

In several of the Western States the Black race never appeared, and in all the Northern States it is declining rapidly. Thus the great question of its future condition is confined within a narrow circle, where it becomes less formidable, though no easier to solve.
The farther south we go, the more difficult it becomes to abolish slavery with advantage; and this arises from several physical causes that are important to point out.

The first of these causes is the climate. It is well known that the closer Europeans come to the tropics, the more they suffer from labor. Many Americans even claim that within a certain latitude the exertions a Black man can make without danger are fatal to them; *o but I do not think that this opinion, which is so convenient for the idleness of the inhabitants of southern regions, is confirmed by experience. The southern parts of the Union are not hotter than the South of Italy and of Spain; *p and it may be asked why the European cannot work as well there as in those two countries. If slavery has been abolished in Italy and in Spain without destroying the masters, why should the same thing not happen in the Union? I cannot believe that nature has forbidden Europeans in Georgia and the Floridas, on pain of death, to raise their means of subsistence from the soil; but their labor would unquestionably be more tiresome and less productive for them than for the inhabitants of New England. Since the free workman thus loses part of his superiority over the slave in the Southern States, there are fewer inducements to abolish slavery.

o [ This is true of the places where rice is cultivated; rice grounds, which are unhealthy in all countries, are particularly dangerous in regions exposed to the rays of a tropical sun. Europeans would not find it easy to cultivate the soil in that part of the New World if it had to be made to produce rice; but may they not live without rice grounds?]
p [ These States are nearer to the equator than Italy and Spain, but the temperature of the continent of America is very much lower than that of Europe.

The Spanish government once had a certain number of peasants from the Azores transported to a district of Louisiana called Attakapas, as an experiment. These settlers still cultivate the soil without the help of slaves, but their industry is so sluggish that it barely supplies their most necessary wants.]

All the plants of Europe grow in the northern parts of the Union; the South has special products of its own. It has been observed that slave labor is a very expensive way of cultivating corn. The farmer of corn land in a country where slavery is unknown keeps a small number of laborers in his service all the time, and at seed time and harvest he hires several additional hands, who live at his expense only for a short period. But the farmer in a slave State has to keep a large number of slaves all year round, in order to sow his fields and bring in his crops, although their services are needed for only a few weeks. Slaves cannot wait until they are hired and support themselves by their own labor in the meantime, as free laborers do; to have their services, they must be bought. Slavery, apart from its general disadvantages, is therefore even less suited to countries where corn is grown than to those that produce other kinds of crops. The cultivation of tobacco, of cotton, and especially of sugar cane, on the other hand, demands constant attention; and women and children are employed in it, whose services are of little use in growing wheat. Thus slavery is naturally better suited to the countries from which these products come. Tobacco, cotton, and sugar cane are grown exclusively in the South, and they are among the principal sources of wealth of those States. If slavery were abolished, the inhabitants of the South would be forced to choose between two alternatives. Either they would have to change their system of cultivation, and then they would come into competition with the more active and more experienced inhabitants of the North; or, if they kept growing the same produce without slave labor, they would have to face the competition of the other Southern States that might still keep their slaves. Thus there are particular reasons for maintaining slavery in the South that do not operate in the North.

But there is yet another motive, more compelling than all the others. Strictly speaking, the South could abolish slavery; but how would it rid its territory of the Black population? Slaves and slavery are driven from the North by the same law, but this twofold result cannot be hoped for in the South.

The arguments I have given, showing that slavery is more natural and more profitable in the South than in the North, are enough to prove that slaves must be far more numerous in the southern districts. It was to the southern settlements that the first Africans were brought, and it is there that the greatest number of them have always been imported. As we advance toward the South, the prejudice that sanctions idleness grows stronger. In the States nearest the tropics there is not a single white laborer; Black people are consequently much more numerous in the South than in the North. And, as I have already observed, this disproportion grows daily, since Black people are transferred to one part of the Union as soon as slavery is abolished in the other. Thus the Black population increases in the South not only by its natural fertility but by the forced emigration of Black people from the North; and the African race has causes of increase in the South very similar to those that so powerfully speed the growth of the European race in the North.

In the State of Maine there is one Black person in 300 inhabitants; in Massachusetts, one in 100; in New York, two in 100; in Pennsylvania, three in the same number; in Maryland, thirty-four; in Virginia, forty-two; and lastly, in South Carolina, *q fifty-five percent. Such was the proportion of the Black population to the whites in the year 1830. But the proportion keeps changing: it falls steadily in the North and rises in the South.

It is clear that the southernmost States of the Union cannot abolish slavery without running very great dangers, ones the North had no reason to fear when it freed its Black population. We have already described how the Northern States manage the transition from slavery to freedom: they keep the present generation in chains and set their descendants free. In this way Black people are brought into society gradually. While the men who might abuse their freedom remain in servitude, those who are freed can learn the art of being free before they become their own masters. But this method would be hard to apply in the South. To declare that all Black people born after a certain date shall be free is to introduce the principle and the idea of liberty into the heart of slavery. The Black people whom the law keeps enslaved, while their children are released from that condition, are astonished at so unequal a fate, and their astonishment is only the prelude to impatience and resentment. From then on, slavery loses in their eyes the kind of moral power it drew from time and habit; it is reduced to a plain abuse of force. The Northern States had nothing to fear from this contrast, because Black people there were few and the white population was very large. But if this faint dawn of freedom were to show two million men their true position, the oppressors would have reason to tremble. Once they had freed the children of their slaves, the Europeans of the Southern States would very soon be obliged to extend the same benefit to the entire Black population.

In the North, as I have already remarked, a twofold migration follows the abolition of slavery, or even precedes it when circumstances have made abolition likely. The slaves leave the country to be transported southward, and the whites of the Northern States, along with emigrants from Europe, hurry to fill their place. But these two causes cannot work in the same way in the Southern States. On the one hand, the mass of slaves is too great for anyone to expect that they could ever be removed from the country. On the other hand, the Europeans and the Anglo-Americans of the North are afraid to settle in a country where labor has not yet been restored to its rightful honor. Besides, they very justly regard the States in which Black people equal or outnumber whites as exposed to very great dangers, and they refrain from directing their energies there.

Thus the people of the South could not, like their Northern countrymen, introduce the slaves gradually to freedom by abolishing slavery. They have no way of noticeably reducing the Black population, and they would be left without support to restrain its excesses. So within a few years a great population of free Black people would exist in the heart of a white nation of equal size.

The same abuses of power that still sustain slavery would then become the source of the most alarming perils the white population of the South might have to fear. At present the descendants of the Europeans are the sole owners of the land, the absolute masters of all labor, and the only people who possess wealth, knowledge, and arms. The Black man has none of these advantages, but he gets by without them because he is a slave. If he were free and had to provide for his own subsistence, would it be possible for him to go without these things and still stay alive? Or would not the very instruments of the white man’s present superiority, while slavery lasts, expose him to a thousand dangers if slavery were abolished?

As long as the Black man remains a slave, he can be kept in a condition not very far from that of the animals. But with his liberty he cannot fail to acquire enough instruction to appreciate his misfortunes and to see a remedy for them. Moreover, there is a peculiar principle of relative justice that is very firmly planted in the human heart. People are struck much more forcibly by inequalities within the same class than by those between different classes. It is easier for them to accept slavery than to allow several million citizens to live under a load of eternal infamy and hereditary wretchedness. In the North the population of freed Black people feels these hardships and resents these indignities, but its numbers and its power are small; in the South it would be numerous and strong.

Once it is admitted that whites and emancipated Black people live on the same territory as two foreign communities, it is easy to see that the future holds only two alternatives: Black people and whites must either separate completely or mingle completely. I have already stated my conviction about the latter. *r I do not imagine that the white and Black races will ever live on an equal footing in any country. But I believe the difficulty to be even greater in the United States than elsewhere. An isolated individual may overcome the prejudices of religion, of country, or of race, and if that individual is a king he may bring about surprising changes in society; but a whole people cannot rise, as it were, above itself. A despot who made the Americans and their former slaves bear the same yoke might perhaps succeed in blending their races. But as long as the American democracy remains at the head of affairs, no one will undertake so difficult a task, and it can be foreseen that the freer the white population of the United States becomes, the more isolated it will remain. *s

I have observed earlier that the mixed race is the true bond of union between the Europeans and the Native Americans. In the same way, people of mixed race are the true means of transition between the white and the Black man, so that wherever they are numerous, the intermixture of the two races is not impossible. In some parts of America the European and Black races have crossed so much that it is rare to meet a man who is entirely Black or entirely white. When they have reached this point, the two races may truly be said to be combined, or rather to have been absorbed into a third race, which is connected with both without being identical with either.

Of all the Europeans, the English are the ones who have mixed least with Black people. More people of mixed race are seen in the South of the Union than in the North, but they are still infinitely scarcer than in any other European colony. They are by no means numerous in the United States; they have no strength of their own, and when quarrels arising from differences of color break out, they generally side with the whites, just as the lackeys of the great in Europe take on the contemptuous airs of the nobility toward the lower orders.

The pride of origin natural to the English is singularly increased by the personal pride that democratic liberty fosters among the Americans. The white citizen of the United States is proud of his race and proud of himself. But if whites and Black people do not intermingle in the North of the Union, how would they mix in the South? Can anyone suppose for a moment that an American of the Southern States, placed as he must forever be between the white man with all his physical and moral superiority and the Black man, will ever think of preferring the latter? The Americans of the Southern States have two powerful passions that will always keep them apart: the first is the fear of being made like Black people, their former slaves; the second is the dread of sinking below the whites, their neighbors.

If I were asked to predict what will probably happen at some future time, I would say that the abolition of slavery in the South will, in the ordinary course of things, increase the white population’s repugnance toward people of color. I base this opinion on a similar observation I had already made in the North. I noticed there that the white inhabitants of the North avoid Black people with increasing care as the legal barriers of separation are removed by the legislature. Why should the same result not occur in the South? In the North, whites are deterred from mixing with Black people by fear of an imaginary danger; in the South, where the danger would be real, I cannot imagine that the fear would be less widespread.

Suppose, on the one hand, it is admitted (and the fact is unquestionable) that the Black population keeps accumulating in the extreme South and that it increases more rapidly than the white population. Suppose, on the other hand, it is granted that no one can foresee a time when whites and Black people will be so intermingled as to draw the same benefits from society. Must we not conclude that Black people and whites will sooner or later come to open conflict in the Southern States of the Union? But if one asks what the outcome of the struggle is likely to be, it is easy to see that we can form only a very vague guess at the truth. The human mind may succeed in drawing a wide circle, as it were, that includes the course of future events; but within that circle a thousand different chances and circumstances may steer it in as many different directions, and every picture of the future contains a dim spot that the eye of the understanding cannot penetrate. It appears, however, extremely probable that in the West Indian Islands the white race is destined to be overcome, and the Black population on the continent to share the same fate.

In the West India Islands the white planters are surrounded by an immense Black population. On the continent, Black people are placed between the ocean and an innumerable people that already spreads over them in a dense mass, from the icy borders of Canada to the frontiers of Virginia, and from the banks of the Missouri to the shores of the Atlantic. If the white citizens of North America remain united, we cannot suppose that Black people will escape the destruction that threatens them; they must be subdued by want or by the sword. But the Black population accumulated along the coast of the Gulf of Mexico has a chance of success if the American Union is dissolved when the struggle between the two races begins. If the federal tie were broken, the citizens of the South would be wrong to rely on any lasting help from their Northern countrymen. The Northerners know well that the danger can never reach them, and unless they are compelled to march to the South’s assistance by a formal obligation, it can be foreseen that the sympathy of color will not be enough to spur them to effort.

Yet whenever the conflict may break out, the whites of the South, even if left to their own resources, will enter the contest with an immense superiority in knowledge and in the means of warfare. But Black people will have numerical strength and the energy of despair on their side, and these are powerful resources for men who have taken up arms. The fate of the white population of the Southern States will perhaps be like that of the Moors in Spain. After occupying the land for centuries, it will perhaps be forced to withdraw to the country its ancestors came from, and to leave to Black people the possession of a territory that Providence seems to have destined more particularly for them, since they can live and work in it more easily than whites.

The danger of a conflict between the white and Black inhabitants of the Southern States of the Union — a danger that, however remote, is inevitable — haunts the imagination of the Americans without rest. The people of the North make it a common topic of conversation, although they have no direct injury to fear from the struggle, but they try in vain to devise some means of avoiding the misfortunes they foresee. In the Southern States the subject is not discussed. The planter does not mention the future when talking with strangers; the citizen does not share his apprehensions with his friends; he tries to hide them from himself. But there is something more alarming in the silent forebodings of the South than in the loud fears of the Northern States.

This all-pervading anxiety has given birth to an undertaking that is little known but may change the fate of a portion of the human race. Out of apprehension of the dangers I have just described, a certain number of American citizens have formed a society to export to the coast of Guinea, at their own expense, any free Black people who are willing to escape the oppression to which they are subject. *t In 1820 the society I am speaking of founded a settlement in Africa, at the seventh degree of north latitude, which bears the name of Liberia. The most recent information tells us that 2,500 Black people are gathered there. They have introduced the democratic institutions of America into the country of their forefathers. Liberia has a representative system of government, Black jurymen, Black magistrates, and Black priests; churches have been built, newspapers founded, and, by a strange reversal in the course of the world’s affairs, white men are forbidden to stay within the settlement. *u

They feared that a state of things might arise in Africa like the one on the frontiers of the United States, and that if Black people, like the Native Americans, were brought into collision with a people better educated than themselves, they would be destroyed before they could be civilized.]

This is indeed a strange caprice of fortune. Two hundred years have now passed since the people of Europe set out to tear the Black man from his family and his home in order to carry him to the shores of North America. Today the European settlers are busy sending the descendants of those same Black people back to the Continent from which they were first taken. The barbarous Africans have been brought into contact with civilization in the midst of bondage, and have become acquainted with free political institutions in slavery. Until now Africa has been closed to the arts and sciences of the whites; but perhaps the inventions of Europe will now penetrate those regions, since Africans themselves are introducing them. The settlement of Liberia is founded on a lofty and most fruitful idea; but whatever its results may be for the Continent of Africa, it can offer no remedy to the New World.

In twelve years the Colonization Society has transported 2,500 Black people to Africa; in the same period about 700,000 Black people were born in the United States. Suppose the colony of Liberia were situated so that it could receive thousands of new inhabitants every year, and suppose Black people were in a condition to be sent there with advantage. Suppose the Union gave the society annual subsidies *v and carried Black people to Africa in the vessels of the state. It would still be unable to offset the natural increase of the Black population. And since it could not remove in a year as many people as are born on its territory in the same time, it would fail to halt the growth of the evil, which increases daily in the States. *w The Black race will never leave those shores of the American continent to which it was brought by the passions and vices of Europeans, and it will not disappear from the New World as long as it continues to exist. The inhabitants of the United States may delay the calamities they fear, but they cannot now destroy their efficient cause.

I am obliged to confess that I do not regard the abolition of slavery as a means of warding off the struggle between the two races in the United States. Black people may remain slaves for a long time without complaining; but once they are raised to the level of free men, they will soon revolt at being deprived of all their civil rights, and since they cannot become the equals of the whites, they will soon declare themselves enemies. In the North everything helped to make emancipation easy, and slavery was abolished without putting free Black people in a position that could become formidable, since their number was too small for them ever to claim the exercise of their rights. But the South is different. For the slave-owners of the North, the question of slavery was a question of commerce and manufacturing; for those of the South it is a question of life and death. God forbid that I should try to justify the principle of the enslavement of Black people, as some American writers have done! I only observe that not all the countries that once adopted that execrable principle are equally able to abandon it at present.

When I consider the condition of the South, I can see only two courses open to the white inhabitants of those States: either to emancipate Black people and mingle with them, or, remaining separate from them, to keep them in slavery as long as possible. All intermediate measures seem to me likely to end, and soon, in the most horrible of civil wars, and perhaps in the extermination of one of the two races. This is how the Americans of the South view the question, and they act consistently with it. Since they are determined not to mingle with Black people, they refuse to emancipate them.

It is not that the people of the South regard slavery as necessary to the planter’s wealth. On this point many of them agree with their Northern countrymen in freely admitting that slavery is harmful to their interest. But they are convinced that, however harmful it may be, they hold their lives on no other terms. The education now spreading in the South has convinced the inhabitants that slavery is injurious to the slave-owner, but it has also shown them, more clearly than before, that there is no way of getting rid of its bad consequences. Hence arises a strange contrast: the more the usefulness of slavery is disputed, the more firmly it is established in the laws; and while the principle of servitude is gradually abolished in the North, that very principle gives rise to harsher and harsher consequences in the South.

The legislation of the Southern States concerning slaves presents today such unparalleled atrocities that they suffice to show how radically the laws of humanity have been perverted, and to reveal the desperate position of the community in which that legislation was enacted. The Americans of this part of the Union have not, indeed, increased the hardships of slavery; on the contrary, they have improved the physical condition of the slaves. The only means by which the ancients maintained slavery were fetters and death; the Americans of the South of the Union have discovered more intellectual safeguards for the duration of their power. They have turned their despotism and violence against the human mind. In antiquity, precautions were taken to keep the slave from breaking his chains; today measures are taken to deprive him even of the desire for freedom. The ancients held the bodies of their slaves in bondage, but they placed no restraint on the mind and no check on education; and they acted consistently with their established principle, since slavery then had a natural end, and one day or another the slave might be set free and become the equal of his master. But the Americans of the South, who do not admit that Black people can ever be blended with themselves, have forbidden them, under severe penalties, to be taught to read or write; and since they will not raise them to their own level, they push them down as nearly as possible to that of animals.

The slave had always been allowed the hope of liberty to lighten the hardships of his condition. But the Americans of the South are well aware that emancipation cannot fail to be dangerous when the freed man can never be assimilated to his former master. To give a man his freedom and leave him in wretchedness and disgrace is nothing less than to prepare a future leader of a slave revolt. Moreover, it has long been noticed that the presence of a free Black person vaguely disturbs the minds of his less fortunate brethren and gives them a dim idea of their rights. The Americans of the South have therefore taken measures to prevent slave-owners, in most cases, from emancipating their slaves — not, indeed, by a positive prohibition, but by subjecting that step to various formalities that are hard to satisfy. I happened to meet an old man in the South of the Union who had lived in an illicit relationship with one of his Black female slaves and had had several children by her, who were born the slaves of their father. He had indeed often thought of leaving them at least their liberty in his will; but years had passed without his being able to overcome the legal obstacles to their emancipation, and in the meantime old age had come and he was about to die. He pictured his sons dragged from market to market, passing from a parent’s authority to the rod of a stranger, until these horrible forebodings drove his dying imagination to frenzy. When I saw him he was a prey to all the anguish of despair, and he made me feel how awful is nature’s retribution on those who have broken her laws.

These evils are unquestionably great; but they are the necessary and foreseen consequence of the very principle of modern slavery. When the Europeans chose their slaves from a race different from their own, which many of them considered inferior to the other races of mankind, and which they all rejected with horror at any thought of intimate connection, they must have believed that slavery would last forever. For no intermediate state can be lasting between the excessive inequality produced by servitude and the complete equality that originates in independence. The Europeans did dimly feel this truth, but without acknowledging it even to themselves. Whenever they have had dealings with Black people, their conduct has been dictated either by their interest and pride or by their compassion. They first violated every right of humanity in their treatment of Black people, and afterward they informed them that those rights were precious and inviolable. They pretended to open their ranks to the slaves, but Black people who tried to enter the community were driven back with scorn; and they have been led, carelessly and unintentionally, to accept freedom in place of slavery, without having the courage to be either wholly wicked or wholly just.

Suppose no one can foresee a time when the Americans of the South will mix their blood with that of Black people. Can they then let their slaves go free without putting their own safety at risk? And if they are obliged to keep that race in bondage to save their own families, may they not be excused for using the means best suited to that end? What is happening in the Southern States of the Union strikes me as both the most horrible and the most natural result of slavery. When I see the order of nature overturned, and when I hear the cry of humanity struggling in vain against the laws, my indignation does not fall on the men of our own time who are the instruments of these outrages. I reserve my execration for those who, after a thousand years of freedom, brought slavery back into the world once more.

Whatever efforts the Americans of the South make to maintain slavery, they will not always succeed. Slavery is now confined to a single region of the civilized earth; Christianity attacks it as unjust and political economy as harmful; and it now stands in contrast with democratic liberties and the knowledge of our age. It cannot survive. By the master’s choice or by the slave’s will, it will end; and in either case great calamities may be expected to follow. If liberty is refused to the Black people of the South, they will in the end seize it by force; if it is given, they will before long abuse it. *x

The survival of the existing institutions of the several States depends to some extent on the survival of the Union itself. It is therefore important to begin by inquiring into the probable fate of the Union. One point may indeed be assumed at once: if the present confederation were dissolved, it seems to me beyond dispute that the States now composing it would not return to their original isolated condition, but that several unions would then be formed in place of one. I do not intend to inquire into the principles on which these new unions would probably be established, but only to show what causes may bring about the breakup of the existing confederation.

For this purpose I shall have to retrace some of the steps I have already taken and return to topics I have discussed before. I know the reader may accuse me of repetition, but the importance of the matter still to be treated is my excuse. I would rather say too much than too little to be fully understood, and I prefer to harm the author rather than slight the subject.

The legislators who framed the Constitution of 1789 tried to give the federal power a distinct and preponderating authority. But they were limited by the nature of the task they had undertaken. They were not appointed to constitute the government of a single people, but to regulate the association of several States; and whatever their inclinations might be, they could not avoid dividing the exercise of sovereignty in the end.

To understand the consequences of this division, it is necessary to draw a short distinction among the affairs of government. Some matters are national by their very nature; that is, they affect the nation as a body and can be entrusted only to the man or the assembly of men who most completely represent the entire nation. War and diplomacy may be counted among these. Other matters are provincial by their very nature; that is, they affect only certain localities and can be handled properly only in that locality. The budget of a municipality is an example. Lastly, there are certain matters of a mixed nature, which are national in that they affect all the citizens who make up the nation, and provincial in that the nation itself need not provide for all of them. Such are the rights that regulate the civil and political condition of the citizens. No society can exist without civil and political rights. These rights therefore concern all citizens alike; but it is not always necessary to the existence and prosperity of the nation that these rights be uniform, nor, consequently, that the central authority regulate them.

There are, then, two distinct categories of matters placed under the direction of the sovereign power, and these categories are found in all well-constituted communities, whatever the basis of the political constitution may otherwise be. Between these two extremes lie the matters I have called mixed. Since these matters are neither exclusively national nor entirely provincial, they may be handled by a national or by a provincial government, according to the agreement of the contracting parties, without in any way impairing the contract of association.

The sovereign power is usually formed by the union of separate individuals who make up a people; and individual powers or collective forces, each representing a very small portion of the sovereign authority, are the only elements subject to the general government of their choice. In this case the general government is more naturally called upon to regulate not only the affairs of essential national importance but also those of more local interest, and the local governments are reduced to the small share of sovereign authority indispensable to their prosperity.

But sometimes the sovereign authority is composed of political bodies already organized, by virtue of circumstances that predate their union. In this case the provincial governments take control not only of the affairs that more particularly belong to their province, but of all or part of the mixed affairs mentioned above. For the confederate nations, which were independent sovereign States before their union and still represent a very considerable share of the sovereign power, have consented to cede to the general government only the exercise of those rights indispensable to the Union.

When the national government, besides the prerogatives inherent in its nature, is invested with the right to regulate affairs that relate partly to general and partly to local interests, it has a preponderating influence. Not only are its own rights extensive, but all the rights it does not hold exist only by its sufferance, and it may be feared that its influence will deprive the provincial governments of their natural and necessary prerogatives.

Now suppose the opposite arrangement, in which the provincial governments are given the power to regulate those same affairs of mixed interest. Society then leans the other way. The stronger force sits in the province rather than in the nation, and it is to be feared that the national government may in the end be stripped of the privileges it needs in order to exist.
Independent nations, then, naturally tend toward centralization, and confederations naturally tend toward dismemberment.

All that remains is to apply these general principles to the American Union. The several States necessarily held the right to regulate every affair that is purely provincial. They also kept the right to decide who is competent to act as a citizen in civil and political matters, to regulate the relations of the members of the community with one another, and to dispense justice. These rights are general in nature, yet they do not necessarily belong to a national government. We have seen that the government of the Union has the power to act in the name of the whole nation when the nation must appear as a single, undivided power: in foreign relations, for instance, and in joint resistance to a common enemy. In short, it handles the affairs I have called exclusively national.

At first glance, the Union seems to hold a larger share of sovereignty than the States do. A closer look shows that it holds a smaller one. The Union’s undertakings are more vast, but its influence is felt less often. The provincial governments’ undertakings are comparatively small, but they never stop, and they keep alive the authority behind them. The government of the Union looks after the general interests of the country. Yet the general interests of a people have a very doubtful effect on individual happiness, whereas provincial interests bear immediately on the well-being of the inhabitants. The Union secures the independence and greatness of the nation, which private citizens do not feel directly. The several States, by contrast, preserve each citizen’s liberty, regulate his rights, protect his property, and secure his life and his whole future prosperity.

The federal government stands very far from the people it governs, while the provincial governments are within everyone’s reach and ready to hear the smallest appeal. The central government has behind it the passions of a few superior men who aspire to run it. The provincial governments have behind them the interests of all the second-rate men who can hope for power only inside their own State. These men nevertheless hold the largest share of authority over the people, because they stand closest to the people’s own level. So the Americans have much more to hope for and to fear from the States than from the Union, and, following the natural bent of the human mind, they are more likely to attach themselves to the former than to the latter. On this point their habits and feelings agree with their interests.

Suppose a compact nation divides its sovereignty and adopts a confederate form of government. For a long time the people’s traditions, habits, and mores will conflict with their laws, and those traditions and habits will tend to give the central government more influence than the laws allow it. Now suppose several confederate states unite to form a single nation. The same causes then work in the opposite direction. I have no doubt that if France became a confederate republic like the United States, its government would at first show more energy than the government of the Union does. And if the Union changed its constitution to a monarchy like the French one, I think the American government would need a long time to gain the force that now governs France. When the Anglo-Americans began their national existence, their provincial existence was already old. Necessary ties had formed between the townships and between the individual citizens of each State. The people were used to treating some matters as common to all, and to handling other affairs as concerning only their own particular interests.

The Union is a vast body, and it gives patriotic feeling no definite object to attach to. The State, by contrast, has distinct and limited forms and boundaries. It stands for a certain number of things that its citizens know well and that everyone loves. It is bound up with the soil itself, with the right of property and the affections of home, with the memories of the past, the labors of the present, and the hopes of the future. Patriotism is often only individual egotism extended, and it still turns toward the State; the Union does not arouse it. Thus the interests, habits, and feelings of the people all tend to center political activity in the States rather than in the Union.

One can easily measure the relative strength of the two governments by watching how each performs its functions. When the government of a State has to speak to an individual or to a gathering of individuals, its language is clear and commanding. The federal government uses the same tone with individuals. But as soon as it has any business with a State, it starts to parley. It explains its motives and justifies its conduct, argues and advises, and does anything except command. If doubts arise over the limits of each government’s constitutional powers, the provincial government states its claim boldly and takes quick, vigorous steps to back it up. The government of the Union, meanwhile, reasons. It appeals to the nation’s interests, its good sense, and its glory; it stalls and negotiates, and it will not agree to act until it is driven to the last extremity. At first sight one might easily suppose that the provincial government is the one armed with the nation’s authority, and that Congress speaks for a single State.

The federal government is therefore, whatever precautions its founders took, so weak by nature that it particularly requires the free consent of the governed in order to survive. It is easy to see that its purpose is to help the States carry out, without difficulty, their resolve to stay united. As long as that resolve exists, its authority is great, moderate, and effective. The Constitution equips the government to control individuals and to overcome without trouble whatever obstacles they may try to put in its way. It was by no means established with the possible separation of one or more States from the Union in view.

Suppose the sovereignty of the Union entered into a struggle with that of the States today. One can confidently predict that the Union would lose, and a struggle of that kind is unlikely ever to be seriously attempted. Whenever the federal government meets steady resistance, it gives way. Experience so far shows that a State that has demanded something with perseverance and resolution has always got it, and that when a separate government has plainly refused to act, it has been left to do as it saw fit. *z

If the Union tried to compel the confederate States to obey by force of arms, it would find itself in a position much like England’s during the War of Independence.

No government, however strong, can easily escape the consequences of a principle it has once accepted as the foundation of its constitution. The States formed the Union by voluntary agreement. In uniting, they did not give up their nationality, and they were not reduced to being one and the same people. If one State chose to withdraw from the contract, it would be hard to disprove its right to do so, and the federal government would have no direct way to uphold its claims, whether by force or by right. For the federal government to overcome easily the resistance of any one of its members, one or more of the others would have to have a special stake in the existence of the Union. That has often been the case in the history of confederations.

Suppose that among the States joined by the federal tie, some alone enjoy the main advantages of union, or depend for their prosperity on its lasting. It is certain that these States will always be ready to back the central government when it forces the others to obey. But the government would then be using a force that does not come from itself, and that comes instead from a principle contrary to its nature. States form confederations in order to gain equal advantages from union. In the case just described, the federal government would draw its power from the unequal distribution of those advantages among the States.

Suppose one of the confederate States has gained such a preponderance that it can take exclusive possession of the central authority. It will then treat the other States as subject provinces and will have its own supremacy respected under the borrowed name of the sovereignty of the Union. Great things may be done in the name of the federal government, but in reality that government will have ceased to exist. *b In both cases, the power acting in the confederation’s name grows stronger the further it departs from the natural state and the accepted principles of confederations.

b [ Thus the province of Holland in the republic of the Low Countries, and the Emperor in the Germanic Confederation, have sometimes put themselves in the place of the union and used the federal authority to their own advantage.]

In America the existing Union benefits every State, but it is not indispensable to any one of them. Several of them could break the federal tie without harming the welfare of the rest, though their own prosperity would suffer. The existence and happiness of none of them depend wholly on the present Constitution, so none of them would be inclined to make great personal sacrifices to preserve it. On the other hand, no State seems so far to have its ambition much bound up with keeping the existing Union in being. They certainly do not all have equal influence in the federal councils, but none can hope to lord it over the others or to treat them as inferiors or subjects.

I find it beyond doubt that if any part of the Union seriously wanted to separate from the other States, the rest could not stop it, and indeed would not try. The present Union will last only as long as the States that make it up choose to remain in the confederation. Once this point is granted, the question becomes less difficult. We are not asking whether the States of the existing Union are able to separate. We are asking whether they will choose to stay united.

Of the many reasons that make the existing Union useful to the Americans, two principal ones stand out to an observer. The Americans are, in a sense, alone on their continent, yet their trade makes them neighbors of every nation they deal with. Their isolation is only apparent. They need a certain degree of strength, and they can keep it only by staying united with one another. If the States were to split apart, they would not only reduce the strength they can now show toward foreign nations; they would soon create foreign powers on their own soil. Inland customs barriers would go up, imaginary boundary lines would cut across the valleys, territorial distinctions would restrict the courses of the rivers, and countless hindrances would keep the Americans from exploring the whole of the vast continent that Providence has given them to rule. For now they have no invasion to fear, and so they have no standing armies to maintain and no taxes to levy. If the Union dissolved, all these burdensome measures might soon be required. The Americans therefore have a very strong interest in keeping their Union. On the other hand, one can hardly find any material interest that would now tempt a part of the Union to break away from the rest.

Looking at a map of the United States, we see the chain of the Alleghany Mountains running from northeast to southwest across nearly a thousand miles of country. We are tempted to think Providence meant to raise between the valley of the Mississippi and the Atlantic coast one of those natural barriers that cut off contact between peoples and mark the necessary limits of different States. But the Alleghanies average no more than 2,500 feet in height, and their highest point is not above 4,000 feet. Their rounded summits, and the broad valleys hidden in their passes, can be entered easily from several sides. Besides this, the principal rivers that empty into the Atlantic Ocean — the Hudson, the Susquehanna, and the Potomac — all begin beyond the Alleghanies, in an open district that borders the valley of the Mississippi. They leave that region and break through the barrier that seems to turn them westward, and as they wind through the mountains they give people an easy, natural way across. There is no natural barrier anywhere in the regions the Anglo-Americans now inhabit. The Alleghanies, far from separating nations, do not even serve as a frontier between States. New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia take them within their borders, and those States reach as far west of the line as east of it. The territory now held by the twenty-four States of the Union, together with the three great districts that already have inhabitants but have not yet been given the rank of States, covers 1,002,600 square miles, *c which is about five times the size of France. Within these limits the soil, the temperature, and the produce of the country vary enormously. The great extent of territory held by the Anglo-American republics has raised doubts about whether their Union can last. Here we must draw a distinction. In a vast empire, opposing interests sometimes arise in different provinces and often end in open conflict, and then the size of the country does the greatest harm to the power of the State. But if the inhabitants of such vast regions are not divided by opposing interests, the size of the territory may help their prosperity. Unity of government encourages the exchange of the soil’s different products, and it raises their value by making them easier to consume.
