Different interests are indeed easy to find in the different parts of the Union, but I know of none that are hostile to one another. The Southern States are almost wholly agricultural. The Northern States are especially commercial and manufacturing. The Western States are agricultural and manufacturing at once. In the South the crops are tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugar; in the North and West they are wheat and maize. These are different sources of wealth, but union is the means that opens them all to everyone and makes each equally profitable to every district.

The North carries the produce of the Anglo-Americans to every part of the world and brings the world’s produce back to the Union. It plainly has an interest in keeping the confederation as it now stands, so that the number of American producers and consumers stays as large as possible. The North is the most natural go-between linking the South and West of the Union with the rest of the world. It therefore has an interest in the union and prosperity of the South and West, so that they may keep supplying raw materials for its factories and cargoes for its ships.

The South and the West, for their part, have an even more direct interest in preserving the Union and in the North’s prosperity. Most of the South’s produce is shipped overseas, so the South and the West both depend on the North’s commercial resources. They also have an interest in the Union keeping a powerful fleet to protect them effectively. The South and West own no ships, but they cannot refuse to pay willingly toward the navy’s expenses. If the fleets of Europe blockaded the ports of the South and the mouth of the Mississippi, what would become of the rice of the Carolinas, the tobacco of Virginia, and the sugar and cotton grown in the Mississippi valley? Every part of the federal budget thus helps to maintain material interests shared by all the confederate States.

Besides this commercial usefulness, the South and the West gain great political advantages from their connection with the North. The South has an enormous slave population, one that is already alarming and will be more formidable still in the future. The Western States lie at the far end of a single valley. All the rivers that cross their territory rise in the Rocky Mountains or the Alleghanies and flow into the Mississippi, which carries them on to the Gulf of Mexico. Their position therefore cuts the Western States off entirely from the traditions of Europe and the civilization of the Old World. So the people of the South have reason to support the Union in order to have its protection against Black people. The people of the West have reason to support it so as not to lose free communication with the rest of the world and be shut up in the wilds of central America. And the North cannot help wanting the Union kept in being, so that it can remain, as it is now, the link between that vast body and the rest of the world.
The material interests of all the parts of the Union, then, are closely tied together. The same is true of those opinions and feelings that may be called the immaterial interests of men.

The people of the United States talk a great deal about their love of country. I confess that I do not rely on that calculating patriotism, which rests on interest and which a change in the interests at stake can wipe out. Nor do I give much weight to the Americans’ words when, in daily conversation, they declare their intention to maintain the federal system their forefathers adopted. A government holds its sway over a great number of citizens far less through the voluntary, reasoned consent of the multitude than through an instinctive and, to some extent, involuntary agreement that comes from similar feelings and resemblances of opinion. I will never grant that men form a social body merely because they obey the same head and the same laws. Society can exist only when a great number of men see a great number of things from the same point of view, hold the same opinions on many subjects, and have the same thoughts and impressions suggested to them by the same events.

An observer who examines the present condition of the United States by this principle will readily see that, although the citizens are divided into twenty-four distinct sovereignties, they still form a single people. He may perhaps be led to think that the Anglo-American Union is more truly a society than certain nations of Europe that live under the same laws and the same prince.

The Anglo-Americans belong to several religious sects, yet they all look at religion in the same way. They do not always agree about which measures best serve good government, and they differ over some of the forms of government worth adopting. But they are unanimous about the general principles that should govern human society. From Maine to the Floridas, and from the Missouri to the Atlantic Ocean, the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. Everywhere the same ideas are held about liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, trial by jury, and the responsibility of the agents of government.

If we leave their political and religious opinions and turn to the moral and philosophical principles that shape the actions of daily life and guide their conduct, we find the same uniformity. The Anglo-Americans *d recognize the absolute moral authority of the community’s reason, just as they recognize the political authority of the mass of citizens, and they hold that public opinion is the surest judge of what is allowed or forbidden, true or false. Most of them believe that a man will be led to do what is just and good by following his own self-interest properly understood. They hold that every man is born with the right to govern himself, and that no one has the right to force his fellow creatures to be happy. They all have a lively faith in human perfectibility. They think that the spread of knowledge must have good effects and that ignorance must have fatal ones. They all see society as a body that is improving, and humanity as a changing scene in which nothing is, or should be, permanent. And they admit that what seems good to them today may be replaced tomorrow by something better. I do not offer all these opinions as true. I cite them as characteristic of the Americans.

d [ I hardly need point out that by the expression Anglo-Americans I mean only the great majority of the nation; for a certain number of isolated individuals are of course to be found holding very different opinions.]

These shared opinions are not all that unites the Anglo-Americans. A common feeling of pride also sets them apart from every other nation. For the last fifty years, no effort has been spared to persuade the people of the United States that they alone are religious, enlightened, and free. They see that for the moment their own democratic institutions succeed while those of other countries fail. They therefore form an inflated opinion of their own superiority, and they are not far from believing that they belong to a different race of mankind.

The dangers that threaten the American Union come not from diversity of interests or opinions but from the differing characters and passions of the Americans. The men who live across the vast territory of the United States are almost all descended from one common stock. But climate, and above all slavery, have gradually produced very striking differences between the British settler in the Southern States and the British settler in the North. In Europe it is generally believed that slavery has set the interests of one part of the Union against those of another. I did not find this to be so at all. Slavery has not created interests in the South opposed to those of the North. What it has done is change the character and habits of the South’s native-born people.

I have already explained how slavery has affected the commercial ability of the Southern Americans, and the same influence extends equally to their mores. The slave is a servant who never protests and who submits to everything without complaint. He may sometimes murder his master, but he never stands up to him. In the South no family is too poor to own slaves. From his earliest years the Southern citizen holds a kind of domestic dictatorship. The first idea he gets in life is that he was born to command, and the first habit he forms is that of being obeyed without resistance. His upbringing thus tends to make him haughty and hasty: irascible, violent, and ardent in his desires, impatient with obstacles, yet easily discouraged if he fails at his first attempt.

The American of the Northern States grows up with no slaves around him, and not even free servants to wait on him, and he usually has to provide for his own needs. As soon as he enters the world, the idea of necessity presses on him from every side. He quickly learns exactly where the natural limit of his authority lies. He never expects to subdue by force those who resist him, and he knows that the surest way to win the support of his fellow creatures is to earn their favor. So he becomes patient, thoughtful, tolerant, slow to act, and steady in his plans.

In the Southern States the more pressing needs of life are always provided for. The people there are not occupied with the material cares of life, since others always attend to them, and their imagination turns to more captivating and less definite objects. The Southerner loves grandeur, luxury, and renown, gaiety and pleasure, and above all idleness. Nothing forces him to exert himself to make a living, and since he has no necessary occupation, he gives in to laziness and does not even try what would be useful.

In the North, however, equality of fortunes and the absence of slavery plunge people into the same cares of daily life that the white population of the South looks down on. From infancy they are taught to fight want and to put comfort above every pleasure of the mind or heart. Imagination is stifled by the petty details of life, and ideas grow fewer and less general, though far more practical and precise. Since prosperity is the only aim of their efforts, they reach it superbly. Nature and mankind are turned to the best financial account, and society is cleverly made to serve the welfare of each of its members, so that individual egotism becomes the source of general happiness.

The Northerner has not only experience but knowledge, and yet he values the pleasures of knowledge very little. To him it is a means to an end, and he is eager only to seize its most profitable uses. The Southerner is more inclined to act on impulse. He is cleverer, more open, more generous, more intellectual, and more brilliant. The Northerner has more activity, common sense, information, and general ability, and he has the characteristic virtues and vices of the middle classes. The Southerner has the tastes, prejudices, weaknesses, and magnanimity of every aristocracy. Take two men who share a society and have the same interests and, to some degree, the same opinions, but who differ in character, in what they have learned, and in their style of civilization. They will probably not agree. The same holds for a society of nations. Slavery, then, does not attack the American Union directly through its interests, but indirectly through its mores.

Thirteen States gave their assent to the federal contract in 1790. The Union now has thirty-four members. The population, nearly 4,000,000 in 1790, more than tripled in forty years and reached nearly 13,000,000 in 1830. *e Changes on this scale cannot take place without some danger.

A society of nations, like a society of individuals, owes its main chances of lasting to the wisdom of its members, their individual weakness, and their small number. The Americans who leave the Atlantic coast and plunge into the western wilderness are adventurers who cannot bear restraint, who are greedy for wealth, and who are often men driven out of the States where they were born. When they reach the wilds, they are strangers to one another, and they have no traditions, no family feeling, and no example to hold their excesses in check. Among them the rule of law is weak, and that of morality weaker still. The settlers who keep filling the Mississippi valley are thus in every respect far inferior to the Americans of the older parts of the Union. Yet they already have great influence in its councils, and they come to govern the commonwealth before they have learned to govern themselves. *f
f [ This is indeed only a temporary danger. I have no doubt that in time society will acquire as much stability and regularity in the West as it already has on the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.]

The weaker each party to a contract is individually, the better the chances that the contract will last, since their safety then depends on staying united. In 1790 the most populous of the American republics had fewer than 500,000 inhabitants. *g Each felt how insignificant it was as an independent people, and that feeling made it easier to comply with the federal authority. But consider a confederate State like New York, which counts 2,000,000 inhabitants and covers a territory equal to a quarter of France. *h Such a State feels its own strength. It may keep supporting the Union because the Union helps its prosperity, but it no longer sees the Union as necessary to its existence. And while it remains a party to the federal compact, it soon aims at preponderance in the federal assemblies. The likelihood of unanimity among the States diminishes as their number grows. Today the interests of the different parts of the Union do not conflict. But who can foresee the many changes still to come in a country where towns are founded from one day to the next, and States almost from one year to the next?
g [ Pennsylvania contained 431,373 inhabitants in 1790 [and 5,258,014 in 1890.]]
h [ The area of the State of New York is 49,170 square miles. [See U. S. census report of 1890.]]

Ever since the British colonies were first settled, their population has roughly doubled every twenty-two years. I can see nothing likely to halt this steady growth of the Anglo-American population during the next hundred years. Before that time is up, I believe, the territories and dependencies of the United States will hold more than 100,000,000 inhabitants and be divided into forty States. *i I grant that these 100,000,000 men will have no hostile interests. I even suppose that they all have an equal stake in keeping the Union. Still, I hold that with 100,000,000 men and forty distinct nations of unequal strength, the survival of the federal government can only be a lucky accident.

i [ If the population continues to double every twenty-two years, as it has done for the last two hundred years, the number of inhabitants in the United States in 1852 will be twenty millions; in 1874, forty-eight millions; and in 1896, ninety-six millions. The territory already occupied can easily hold this number of inhabitants. One hundred millions of men spread over the surface of the twenty-four States and the three dependencies that make up the Union would give only 762 inhabitants to the square league. This is far below the mean population of France, which is 1,063 to the square league, or of England, which is 1,457; and it would even be below the population of Switzerland, for that country, despite its lakes and mountains, has 783 inhabitants to the square league. However much faith I have in human perfectibility, I will refuse to believe that a government can last when it is asked to hold together forty different peoples spread over a territory half the size of Europe, to prevent all rivalry, ambition, and conflict among them, and to direct their independent activity toward the same ends. I will keep refusing until human nature changes and men are wholly transformed.

But the greatest danger the Union faces from its growth comes from the constant shifting of its internal strength. From Lake Superior to the Gulf of Mexico the distance runs from the 47th to the 30th degree of latitude, more than 1,200 miles in a straight line. The frontier of the United States winds along this whole immense line, sometimes falling inside it, but more often reaching far beyond it into the wilderness. It has been calculated that the whites advance an average of seventeen miles a year along this entire vast boundary. *j Now and then they meet obstacles: an unproductive district, a lake, or a Native American nation they did not expect to find. The advancing column then halts for a while. Its two ends fall back on themselves, and as soon as they have joined up again, they move forward. This slow, unbroken progress of the European race toward the Rocky Mountains has the solemnity of a providential event. It is like a flood of men that keeps rising and is driven forward every day by the hand of God.
j [ See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 105.]

Within this first line of conquering settlers, towns are built and great States founded. In 1790 only a few thousand pioneers were scattered along the valleys of the Mississippi. Today those valleys hold as many people as the entire Union held in 1790. Their population is nearly 4,000,000. *k The city of Washington was founded in 1800 at the very center of the Union. But so much has changed that it now lies at one of the extremities, and the delegates from the most remote Western States already have to make a journey as long as the one from Vienna to Paris. *l
l [ The distance from Jefferson, the capital of the State of Missouri, to Washington is 1,019 miles. (“American Almanac,” 1831, p. 48.)]

All the States are carried forward together along the road to fortune, but they naturally do not all grow and prosper at the same rate. In the North, the outlying branches of the Alleghany chain run all the way to the Atlantic Ocean and form spacious roadsteads and ports that vessels of the greatest burden can always enter. But from the Potomac to the mouth of the Mississippi the coast is sandy and flat. In this part of the Union the mouths of nearly all the rivers are blocked, and the few harbors among the lagoons offer ships much shallower water and far fewer commercial advantages than those of the North.

This first natural cause of inferiority is joined by another that comes from the laws. We have already seen that slavery, which has been abolished in the North, still exists in the South, and I have pointed out its fatal consequences for the prosperity of the planter himself.

The North is therefore superior to the South in both commerce *m and manufacturing, and the natural result is a more rapid growth of population and wealth within its borders. The States on the shores of the Atlantic Ocean are already half-peopled. Most of the land there has an owner, so these districts cannot take in as many emigrants as the Western States, where a boundless field is still open to their efforts. The valley of the Mississippi is far more fertile than the Atlantic coast. This reason, added to all the others, drives Europeans westward — a fact that can be demonstrated rigorously with figures. The total population of all the United States has roughly tripled over forty years. But in the new States next to the Mississippi, the population has grown thirty-one-fold in the same period. *n

The relative position of the central federal power is continually shifting. Forty years ago most of the citizens of the Union lived on the Atlantic coast, in the area around the spot where Washington now stands. But the great body of the people is now moving inland and to the north, so that within twenty years the majority will undoubtedly be on the western side of the Alleghanies. If the Union continues to exist, the basin of the Mississippi is clearly marked out, by its fertility and its size, as the future center of the Federal Government. In thirty or forty years that region will have taken the rank that naturally belongs to it. It is easy to calculate that its population, compared to that of the Atlantic coast, will be, in round numbers, as 40 to 11. In a few years the States that founded the Union will lose the direction of its policy, and the population of the valley of the Mississippi will predominate in the federal assemblies.

This constant shift of federal power and influence toward the northwest shows itself every ten years, when a general census is taken and the number of delegates each State sends to Congress is set anew. *o In 1790 Virginia had nineteen representatives in Congress. That number kept rising until 1813, when it reached twenty-three; from then on it declined, and in 1833 Virginia elected only twenty-one representatives. *p Over the same period the State of New York moved in the opposite direction: in 1790 it had ten representatives in Congress; in 1813, twenty-seven; in 1823, thirty-four; and in 1833, forty. The State of Ohio had only one representative in 1803, and in 1833 it already had nineteen.

It is necessary to explain how the number of representatives for a State can fall when the State’s population, far from shrinking, is actually growing. I take the State of Virginia, which I have already mentioned, as my point of comparison. The number of Virginia’s representatives in 1823 was proportional to the total number of representatives of the Union and to the ratio of its population to that of the whole Union. In 1833 the number of Virginia’s representatives was likewise proportional to the total number of representatives of the Union and to the ratio of its population, enlarged over ten years, to the enlarged population of the Union over the same time. The new number of Virginian representatives will then stand to the old number, on the one hand, as the new total number of representatives stands to the old; and, on the other hand, as the growth of Virginia’s population stands to the growth of the whole population of the country. Thus, if the growth of the smaller country’s population stands to that of the larger in exact inverse ratio to the proportion between the new and old totals of representatives, the number of Virginia’s representatives will stay the same. And if the growth of the Virginian population stands to that of the whole Union in a weaker ratio than the new number of the Union’s representatives to the old number, the number of Virginia’s representatives must fall. It is hard to imagine a lasting union between a rich, strong people and a poor, weak one, even if it were proved that the strength and wealth of the one are not the causes of the weakness and poverty of the other. But union is harder still to maintain when one party is losing strength and the other is gaining it. This rapid and disproportionate growth of certain States threatens the independence of the others. New York, with its 2,000,000 inhabitants and its forty representatives, might perhaps succeed in dictating to the other States in Congress. But even if the more powerful States make no attempt to overbear the lesser ones, the danger remains, for the possibility of the act matters almost as much as the act itself. The weak generally distrust the justice and the reason of the strong. The States that grow less rapidly than the others look with envy and suspicion on those that fortune favors more. Hence come the deep-seated uneasiness and vague agitation that can be observed in the South, and that contrast so sharply with the confidence and prosperity common to other parts of the Union. I am inclined to think that the hostile measures taken by the Southern provinces on a recent occasion are due to no other cause. Of all Americans, the inhabitants of the Southern States have the greatest interest in maintaining the Union; they would surely suffer most from being left to themselves; and yet they are the only citizens who threaten to break the bond of confederation. But it is easy to see that the South has given the Union four Presidents, Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe; that it perceives it is losing its federal influence; that the number of its representatives in Congress is shrinking from year to year, while those of the Northern and Western States are growing; and that the South, which is peopled with ardent and irascible men, is becoming more and more irritated and alarmed. Its citizens reflect on their present position and remember their past influence, with the melancholy uneasiness of men who suspect oppression. If they find a law of the Union that is not unequivocally favorable to their interests, they protest against it as an abuse of force; and if their ardent remonstrances go unheard, they threaten to leave an association that loads them with burdens while it deprives them of their due profits. “The tariff,” said the inhabitants of Carolina in 1832, “enriches the North, and ruins the South; for if this were not the case, to what can we attribute the continually increasing power and wealth of the North, with its inclement skies and arid soil; while the South, which may be styled the garden of America, is rapidly declining?” *q
q [ See the report of its committee to the Convention which proclaimed the nullification of the tariff in South Carolina.]

If the changes I have described were gradual, so that each generation at least had time to pass away along with the order of things it had lived under, the danger would be smaller. But the progress of society in America is precipitate and almost revolutionary. The same citizen may live to see his State take the lead in the Union and then become powerless in the federal assemblies; and an Anglo-American republic has been known to grow as fast as a man passing from birth and infancy to maturity in thirty years. It must not be imagined, however, that States that lose their predominance also lose their population or their wealth. Their prosperity is not halted, and they even go on growing faster than any kingdom in Europe. *r But they believe themselves impoverished because their wealth does not grow as fast as their neighbors’, and they think their power is lost because they have suddenly run up against a power greater than their own. *s Thus they are hurt more in their feelings and passions than in their interests. But that is amply enough to endanger the maintenance of the Union. If kings and peoples had only ever looked to their true interests since the beginning of the world, the name of war would scarcely be known among mankind.

r [ The population of a country is surely the first element of its wealth. (See the “American Almanac,” 1832, p. 162) But the population of Russia, which grows faster than that of any other European country, increases in ten years at only 9.5 percent; in France, at seven percent; and in Europe in general, at 4.7 percent. So the prosperity of the United States is the source of the gravest dangers that threaten them. It tends to produce, in some of the confederate States, the feverish excitement that comes with fast-growing fortunes, and to awaken in others the envy, mistrust, and regret that usually follow when such fortunes are lost. The Americans watch this extraordinary and hurried progress with exultation, but they would be wiser to watch it with sorrow and alarm. The Americans of the United States are bound to become one of the greatest nations in the world. Their offshoot will cover almost all of North America, and the continent they live on is their dominion, which cannot slip away from them. What drives them to seize it so soon? Riches, power, and renown will certainly be theirs someday, yet they rush toward their fortune as though only a moment were left to make it their own.

I think I have shown that the existence of the present confederation depends entirely on the continued assent of all the confederates, and, starting from this principle, I have inquired into the causes that may lead the several States to separate from the others. The Union may, however, perish in two different ways. One of the confederate States may choose to withdraw from the compact and so forcibly sever the federal tie; most of my remarks so far apply to this supposition. Or the authority of the Federal Government may be gradually eroded by the simultaneous tendency of the united republics to take back their independence. The central power, stripped one by one of all its prerogatives and reduced to impotence by tacit consent, would become unable to fulfill its purpose, and the second Union would perish, like the first, from a kind of senile incapacity. The gradual weakening of the federal tie, which may finally lead to the dissolution of the Union, is a separate matter, and it may produce a variety of lesser consequences before it brings about so violent a change. The confederation might still subsist even if its government were reduced to such a state of inanition that it paralyzed the nation, caused internal anarchy, and checked the general prosperity of the country.

Having investigated the causes that may lead the Anglo-Americans to disunite, it is important to ask whether, if the Union continues to exist, their government will widen or narrow its sphere of action, and whether it will become more energetic or weaker.

The Americans are evidently disposed to view their future condition with alarm. They see that in most nations of the world the exercise of the rights of sovereignty tends to fall under the control of a few individuals, and they are dismayed by the idea that the same will happen in their own country. Even statesmen feel these fears, or pretend to; for in America centralization is by no means popular, and there is no surer way of courting the majority than to inveigh against the encroachments of the central power. The Americans do not notice that the countries where this alarming tendency to centralization exists are inhabited by a single people, while the fact that the Union is composed of different confederate communities is enough to defeat all the inferences that might be drawn from analogous circumstances. I confess that I am inclined to consider the fears of a great number of Americans as purely imaginary; and far from sharing their dread of power being consolidated in the hands of the Union, I think that the Federal Government is visibly losing strength.
To prove this assertion I shall not turn to any remote events, but to circumstances that I have witnessed myself and that belong to our own time.

A careful look at what is going on in the United States will easily convince us that two opposite tendencies exist in that country, like two distinct currents flowing in opposite directions in the same channel. The Union has now existed for forty-five years, and in that time a vast number of provincial prejudices, which at first were hostile to its power, have died away. The patriotic feeling that attached each American to his native State has become less exclusive, and the different parts of the Union have become more closely connected the better they have come to know each other. The post, *t that great instrument of intellectual communication, now reaches into the backwoods, and steamboats have established daily connections between the different points of the coast. An inland navigation of unexampled speed carries goods up and down the rivers of the country. *u To these advantages of nature and art we may add those restless cravings, that busy-mindedness, and that love of money, which constantly drive the American into active life and bring him into contact with his fellow citizens. He crosses the country in every direction; he visits all the various populations of the land; and there is not a province in France whose natives know each other as well as the 13,000,000 men who cover the territory of the United States.

t [ In 1832 the district of Michigan, which has only 31,639 inhabitants and is still nearly unexplored wilderness, already had 940 miles of mail-roads. The territory of Arkansas, which is even less settled, was already crossed by 1,938 miles of mail-roads. (See the report of the General Post Office, November 30, 1833.) The postage on newspapers alone in the whole Union came to $254,796.]

u [ In the ten years from 1821 to 1831, 271 steamboats were launched on the rivers that water the valley of the Mississippi alone. In 1829, 259 steamboats existed in the United States. (See Legislative Documents, No. 140, p. 274.)]

But as the Americans intermingle, they come to resemble each other more. The differences that result from their climate, their origin, and their institutions grow smaller, and they all draw nearer and nearer to a common type. Every year, thousands of men leave the North to settle in different parts of the Union. They bring with them their faith, their opinions, and their customs; and as they are better educated than the men among whom they are about to live, they soon rise to the head of affairs and shape society to their own advantage. This continual emigration from the North to the South is particularly favorable to the fusion of all the different provincial characters into one national character. The civilization of the North appears to be the common standard to which the whole nation will one day be assimilated.

The commercial ties that unite the confederate States are strengthened by the Americans’ growing manufactures, and the union that began to exist in their opinions gradually becomes part of their habits. The passage of time has swept away the bugbear fears that haunted the imaginations of citizens in 1789. The federal power has not become oppressive; it has not destroyed the independence of the States; it has not subjected the confederates to monarchical institutions; and the Union has not made the lesser States dependent on the larger ones. Instead the confederation has gone on growing in population, wealth, and power. I am therefore convinced that the natural obstacles to the continuance of the American Union are not as powerful at present as they were in 1789, and that the enemies of the Union are not as numerous.

Nevertheless, a careful examination of the history of the United States over the last forty-five years will readily convince us that the federal power is declining, and it is not hard to explain the causes of this phenomenon. *v When the Constitution of 1789 was promulgated, the nation was a prey to anarchy. The Union that followed this confusion aroused much dread and much animosity, but it was warmly supported because it met a pressing need. So although it was more attacked then than it is now, the federal power soon reached the maximum of its authority, as usually happens with a government that triumphs after having braced its strength in the struggle. At that time the interpretation of the Constitution seemed to extend rather than restrain federal sovereignty, and in several respects the Union presented the appearance of a single, undivided people directed in its foreign and internal policy by a single government. But to reach this point the people had risen, to a certain extent, above itself.
v [ [Since 1861 the movement is certainly in the opposite direction, and the federal power has largely increased, and tends to further increase.]]

The Constitution had not destroyed the distinct sovereignty of the States, and all communities, of whatever kind, are driven by a secret propensity to assert their independence. This propensity is even stronger in a country like America, where every village forms a kind of republic accustomed to managing its own affairs. It therefore cost the States an effort to submit to federal supremacy, and all efforts, however successful, necessarily subside along with the causes that gave rise to them.

As the Federal Government consolidated its authority, America resumed its rank among the nations, peace returned to its frontiers, and public credit was restored. Confusion gave way to a settled state of things, which favored the full and free exercise of industrious enterprise. This very prosperity made the Americans forget the cause to which it was owed; and once the danger had passed, the energy and patriotism that had enabled them to face it disappeared from among them. No sooner were they freed from the cares that oppressed them than they easily returned to their ordinary habits and gave themselves up without resistance to their natural inclinations. When a powerful government no longer seemed necessary, they began once more to find it irksome. The Union encouraged general prosperity, and the States were not inclined to abandon the Union; but they wished to make the action of the power that represented it as light as possible. The general principle of Union was adopted, but in every minor detail there was an actual tendency toward independence. The principle of confederation was every day more easily admitted and more rarely applied; so the Federal Government brought about its own decline while it was creating order and peace.

As soon as this tendency of public opinion began to show itself outwardly, the leaders of parties, who live by the passions of the people, began to turn it to their own advantage. The position of the Federal Government then became extremely critical. Its enemies had won the popular favor, and they gained the right to direct its policy by pledging to reduce its influence. From that time forward the government of the Union has invariably been forced to give way whenever it has tried to enter the lists against the governments of the States. And whenever an interpretation of the terms of the Federal Constitution has been called for, that interpretation has most often gone against the Union and in favor of the States.

The Constitution gave the Federal Government the right to provide for the interests of the nation, and it had been held that no other authority was so well suited to superintend the “internal improvements” that affected the prosperity of the whole Union, such as the cutting of canals. But the States were alarmed at a power distinct from their own that could thus dispose of a portion of their territory. They were afraid that the central government would in this way acquire a formidable amount of patronage within their own borders and exercise a degree of influence that they intended to reserve exclusively for their own agents. The Democratic party, which has constantly opposed the growth of federal authority, then accused Congress of usurpation and the Chief Magistrate of ambition. The central government was intimidated by the opposition; it soon acknowledged its error, promising to confine its influence strictly in the future within the circle prescribed to it.

The Constitution gives the Union the right to treat with foreign nations. The Native American tribes on the frontiers of the United States had usually been regarded in this light. As long as these savages consented to retire before the civilized settlers, the federal right was not contested. But as soon as a tribe tried to settle in a fixed place, the adjacent States claimed possession of the lands and the rights of sovereignty over the natives. The central government soon recognized both claims; and after concluding treaties with the tribes as independent nations, it handed them over as subjects to the legislative tyranny of the States. *w

w [ See in the Legislative Documents, already cited where I spoke of the Native Americans, the letter of the President of the United States to the Cherokees, his correspondence on this subject with his agents, and his messages to Congress.]

Some of the States founded on the Atlantic coast extended indefinitely westward, into wild regions that no European had ever entered. The States whose boundaries were irrevocably fixed looked jealously at the unbounded regions that the future would let their neighbors explore. The latter then agreed, in order to conciliate the others and to make union easier, to set their own boundaries and to give up to the confederation at large all the territory beyond those limits. *x From then on the Federal Government became the owner of all the uncultivated lands lying beyond the borders of the thirteen States first confederated. It was given the right to divide and sell them, and the sums derived from this source were reserved exclusively for the public treasury of the Union, to provide funds for purchasing tracts of country from the Native Americans, for opening roads to the remote settlements, and for hastening the advance of civilization as much as possible. In the course of time, however, new States have been formed in the midst of the wilds formerly ceded by the inhabitants of the Atlantic shores. Congress has gone on selling, for the profit of the nation at large, the uncultivated lands these new States contained. But the new States at length asserted that, now that they were fully constituted, they ought to have the exclusive right to use the proceeds of these sales for themselves. As their remonstrances grew more and more threatening, Congress thought fit to deprive the Union of some of the privileges it had hitherto enjoyed; and at the end of 1832 it passed a law by which most of the revenue from the sale of lands was made over to the new western republics, although the lands themselves were not ceded to them. *y

x [ The first act of cession was made by the State of New York in 1780; Virginia, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and South and North Carolina followed this example at different times, and the act of cession of Georgia came as recently as 1802.]
y [ It is true that the President refused his assent to this law, but he fully adopted it in principle. (See Message of December 8, 1833.)]

Even a slight acquaintance with the United States lets one see what the country gains from the bank. The advantages are of several kinds, but one strikes a foreign visitor especially. Banknotes of the United States are accepted at the edge of the wilderness for the same value as in Philadelphia, where the bank carries on its business. *z

z [ The present Bank of the United States was established in 1816 with a capital of $35,000,000; its charter expires in 1836. Last year Congress passed a law to renew it, but the President vetoed the bill. The struggle is still going on with great violence on both sides, and the bank’s speedy fall may easily be foreseen. [It was soon afterwards extinguished by General Jackson.]]

Nevertheless, the Bank of the United States is the target of great animosity. Its directors have openly declared themselves enemies of the President, and they are accused, with some plausibility, of having misused their influence to block his election. The President therefore attacks the institution they represent with the heat of personal hatred, and he is spurred on in his revenge by the belief that the hidden leanings of the majority are on his side. The bank can be seen as the great monetary tie of the Union, just as Congress is the great legislative tie; and the same passions that tend to make the States independent of the central power also help to bring the bank down.

The Bank of the United States always holds a large number of notes issued by the provincial banks, and it can compel them at any time to redeem these in cash. It has nothing to fear from the same demand itself, because its resources are large enough to meet every claim. The provincial banks, however, are thereby threatened and their operations limited, since they may issue only as many notes as is proper for their capital. They put up with this healthy restraint impatiently. The newspapers they have bought, and the President, whose interest makes him their tool, attack the bank with the greatest violence. They stir up the local passions and the blind democratic instinct of the country on their side, and they claim that the bank directors form a permanent aristocratic body whose influence must eventually be felt in the government and must damage the principles of equality on which society in America rests.

The contest between the bank and its opponents is only an incident in the great struggle going on in America between the provinces and the central power, between the spirit of democratic independence and the spirit of gradation and subordination. I do not mean that the enemies of the bank are exactly the same individuals who attack the Federal Government on other points. But I assert that the attacks on the Bank of the United States spring from the same propensities that work against the Federal Government, and that the very numerous opponents of the bank are a deplorable symptom of the declining support for the Federal Government.

The Union has never shown such weakness as in the famous tariff question. *a The wars of the French Revolution and of 1812 had called manufacturing establishments into being in the North of the Union, because they cut off all free communication between America and Europe. When peace came and trade reopened, so that European goods again flowed to the New World, the Americans decided to set up a system of import duties with two aims: to protect their infant manufactures and to pay off the debt run up during the war. The Southern States, which have no manufactures to encourage and are purely agricultural, soon complained of this measure. Those were the plain facts, and I do not claim to examine here whether the complaints were well founded or unjust.
a [ For the details of this affair, see principally the Legislative Documents, 22d Congress, 2d Session, No. 30.]

As early as 1820, South Carolina declared in a petition to Congress that the tariff was “unconstitutional, oppressive, and unjust.” The States of Georgia, Virginia, North Carolina, Alabama, and Mississippi later protested against it with more or less vigor. But Congress, far from listening to these complaints, raised the scale of tariff duties in 1824 and 1828 and recognized anew the principle on which it was founded. A doctrine was then proclaimed in the South, or rather revived, which took the name of Nullification.

I showed in its proper place that the aim of the Federal Constitution was not to form a league but to create a national government. In every case that the Constitution specifies, the Americans of the United States are one undivided people, and on those points the will of the nation is expressed, as in all constitutional nations, through the voice of the majority. Once the majority has announced its decision, the minority has a duty to submit. That is the sound legal doctrine, and the only one consistent with the text of the Constitution and the known intention of its framers.

The partisans of Nullification in the South maintain, on the contrary, that in uniting, the Americans did not intend to reduce themselves to the condition of one and the same people; that they meant to constitute a league of independent States; and that each State consequently keeps its entire sovereignty, if not de facto, at least de jure, and has the right to put its own construction on the laws of Congress and to suspend their execution within its own territory if they are held to be unconstitutional and unjust.

The entire doctrine of Nullification is contained in a sentence spoken by Vice-President Calhoun, the head of that party in the South, before the Senate of the United States in 1833: “The Constitution is a compact to which the States were parties in their sovereign capacity; now, whenever a compact is entered into by parties which acknowledge no tribunal above their authority to decide in the last resort, each of them has a right to judge for itself in relation to the nature, extent, and obligations of the instrument.” It is evident that such a doctrine destroys the very basis of the Federal Constitution and brings back all the evils of the old confederation, from which the Americans were supposed to have been safely delivered.

When South Carolina saw that Congress turned a deaf ear to its remonstrances, it threatened to apply the doctrine of nullification to the federal tariff bill. Congress held to its former system, and at length the storm broke. In the course of 1832 the citizens of South Carolina *b named a national Convention to consult on the extraordinary measures they were called upon to take. On November 24th of the same year this Convention promulgated a law, in the form of a decree, that annulled the federal tariff law, forbade the collection of the duties the law commands, and refused to recognize any appeal to the federal courts. *c This decree was to take effect only in the following February, and it was intimated that if Congress changed the tariff before then, South Carolina might be induced to go no further with her threats; a vague wish was afterwards expressed to submit the question to an extraordinary assembly of all the confederate States.

b [ That is to say, the majority of the people, for the opposing party, called the Union party, always formed a very strong and active minority. Carolina may have about 47,000 electors; 30,000 were in favor of nullification and 17,000 opposed to it.]

c [ This decree was preceded by a report of the committee that drafted it, explaining the motives and object of the law. The following passage occurs in it, p. 34: — “When the rights reserved by the Constitution to the different States are deliberately violated, it is the duty and the right of those States to interfere, in order to check the progress of the evil; to resist usurpation, and to maintain, within their respective limits, those powers and privileges which belong to them as independent sovereign States. If they were destitute of this right, they would not be sovereign. South Carolina declares that she acknowledges no tribunal upon earth above her authority. She has indeed entered into a solemn compact of union with the other States; but she demands, and will exercise, the right of putting her own construction upon it; and when this compact is violated by her sister States, and by the Government which they have created, she is determined to avail herself of the unquestionable right of judging what is the extent of the infraction, and what are the measures best fitted to obtain justice.”]

In the meantime South Carolina armed her militia and prepared for war. But Congress, which had slighted its suppliant subjects, listened to their complaints as soon as they were found to have taken up arms. *d A law was passed under which the tariff duties were to be reduced progressively over ten years, until they were brought so low as not to exceed the amount of revenue the government needed. *e Thus Congress completely abandoned the principle of the tariff and substituted a mere fiscal impost for a system of protective duties. *f The government of the Union, to conceal its defeat, resorted to an expedient very much in vogue with feeble governments. It yielded the point de facto but remained inflexible on the principles in question; and while Congress was altering the tariff law, it passed another bill giving the President extraordinary powers, enabling him to overcome by force a resistance that was by then no longer to be feared.

d [ Congress finally decided to take this step because of the conduct of the powerful State of Virginia, whose legislature offered to act as mediator between the Union and South Carolina. Until then South Carolina had seemed to be completely abandoned, even by the States that had joined in her protests.]
e [ This law was passed on March 2, 1833.]
f [ This bill was introduced by Mr. Clay, and it passed both Houses of Congress in four days by an overwhelming majority.]

But South Carolina would not leave the Union content with these meager trophies of success. The same national Convention that had annulled the tariff law met again and accepted the concession that was offered. At the same time, however, it declared that it held as firmly as ever to the doctrine of Nullification. To prove it, it annulled the law that gave the President extraordinary powers, although it was quite certain that the provisions of that law would never be carried out.

Almost all the disputes I have been describing took place under the presidency of General Jackson, and it cannot be denied that on the tariff question he defended the claims of the Union with vigor and skill. I am nevertheless of the opinion that the conduct of the man who now heads the federal government may be counted among the dangers that threaten its survival.

Some people in Europe have formed an opinion about the influence General Jackson may have on the affairs of his country, and those who have looked more closely into the matter find it highly exaggerated. We have been told that General Jackson has won a number of battles, that he is an energetic man, inclined by nature and by habit to use force, greedy for power, and a despot by temperament. All this may perhaps be true, but the conclusions drawn from it are badly mistaken. People have imagined that General Jackson is determined to establish a dictatorship in America, to introduce a military spirit, and to give the central authority a degree of influence that could not fail to endanger local liberties. But in America the time for such undertakings has not yet come, and neither has the age for men of this kind. If General Jackson had hoped to exercise his authority in this way, he would certainly have lost his political position and put his life at risk. He has accordingly not been so imprudent as to attempt anything of the kind.

Far from wishing to extend federal power, the President belongs to the party that wants to confine it to the bare letter of the Constitution and that never interprets that document in a way favorable to the government of the Union. Far from being a champion of centralization, General Jackson is the instrument of all the jealousies of the States, and the passions of the people that are most hostile to the central government put him in the high office he holds. By constantly flattering those passions he keeps his position and his popularity. General Jackson is the slave of the majority: he yields to its wishes, its inclinations and its demands. Or rather, he anticipates and forestalls them.

Whenever the governments of the States come into conflict with that of the Union, the President is generally the first to doubt his own rights. He almost always goes further than the legislature, and when the extent of federal power is disputed, he takes sides, in a manner of speaking, against himself. He hides his official interests and suppresses his own natural inclinations. This is not because he is naturally weak or hostile to the Union. When the majority ruled against the claims of the supporters of nullification, he put himself at its head, stated the doctrines the nation held clearly and forcefully, and was the first to recommend forceful measures. But General Jackson seems to me, if I may use the American expressions, to be a Federalist by taste and a Republican by calculation.

General Jackson stoops to win the favor of the majority. But once he feels his popularity is secure, he sweeps aside every obstacle in pursuit of the goals the community approves of, or of those it does not view with a jealous eye. He is backed by a power his predecessors never knew, and he tramples on his personal enemies whenever they cross his path with an ease no earlier President ever enjoyed. He takes responsibility for measures that no one before him would have dared to attempt. He even treats the national representatives with a disdain that comes close to insult. He vetoes the laws of Congress, and he often does not bother to answer that powerful body. He is a favorite who sometimes treats his master roughly. The power of General Jackson is constantly growing, but that of the President is declining. In his hands the federal government is strong, but it will pass weakened to his successor.

I am strangely mistaken if the federal government of the United States is not constantly losing strength, gradually withdrawing from public affairs, and narrowing its sphere of action more and more. It is feeble by nature, and now it gives up even the pretense of strength. On the other hand, I thought I noticed in the States a livelier sense of independence and a more decided attachment to local government. The Union is to survive, but only as a shadow. It is to be strong in some cases and weak in all others. In time of war it is to be able to gather the whole strength of the nation and all the resources of the country into its hands, and in time of peace its existence is to be barely noticeable, as if this alternation of weakness and vigor were natural or even possible.

I do not see anything at present that might check this general movement of public opinion, and the causes that gave rise to it continue to operate with the same effect. The change will therefore go on, and it may be predicted that, unless some extraordinary event occurs, the government of the Union will grow weaker every day.

I think, however, that the time is still far off when federal power will be entirely extinguished by its inability to protect itself and to keep the peace in the country. The Union is supported by the customs and the wishes of the people, its results are plain, and its benefits are visible. When people see that the weakness of the federal government endangers the existence of the Union, I have no doubt that a reaction will follow, aimed at increasing its strength.

Of all the federal governments established so far, the government of the United States is the one most naturally destined to act. As long as it is attacked only indirectly, through the interpretation of its laws, and as long as its substance is not seriously altered, a change of opinion, an internal crisis or a war may restore all the vigor it needs. The point I have been most anxious to bring out clearly is simply this. Many people, especially in France, imagine that opinion in the United States is changing in favor of a centralization of power in the hands of the President and Congress. I hold that a contrary tendency can plainly be observed. Far from gaining strength and threatening the sovereignty of the States as it grows older, the federal government is, I maintain, growing weaker and weaker, and it is the sovereignty of the Union alone that is in danger. Such are the facts the present time reveals. The future conceals where this tendency will finally lead, and which events may check, slow or hasten the changes I have described. But I do not pretend to be able to lift the veil that hides them from our sight.
Of the Republican Institutions of the United States, and What Their Chances of Duration Are

The Union is accidental — The republican institutions have better prospects of permanence — A republic is, for the present, the natural state of the Anglo-Americans — Reason for this — To destroy it, all the laws must be changed at the same time, and a great change must take place in customs — Difficulties the Americans experience in creating an aristocracy.

The breakup of the Union might bring war into the heart of the States that are now confederated, along with standing armies, a dictatorship and heavy taxation, and in the end it might endanger the republican institutions. But we ought not to confuse the future prospects of the republic with those of the Union. The Union is an accident that will last only as long as circumstances favor it. A republican form of government, however, seems to me to be the natural state of the Americans, and nothing but the continued action of hostile causes, always working in the same direction, could change it into a monarchy. The Union exists mainly in the law that formed it, and one revolution or one change in public opinion might destroy it forever. But the republic rests on a much deeper foundation.

What is understood by a republican government in the United States is the slow and quiet action of society upon itself. It is an orderly state of things truly founded on the enlightened will of the people. It is a conciliatory government, in which decisions are given time to ripen, are discussed deliberately, and are carried out with mature judgment. Republicans in the United States set a high value on morality, respect religious belief, and acknowledge the existence of rights. They profess to think that a people ought to be moral, religious and temperate in proportion as it is free. What is called the republic in the United States is the tranquil rule of the majority, which, after it has had time to examine itself and to give proof of its existence, is the common source of all the powers of the State. But the power of the majority is not unlimited in itself. In the moral world, humanity, justice and reason enjoy an undisputed supremacy, and in the political world, vested rights are treated with no less deference. The majority recognizes these two barriers. If it now and then oversteps them, it is because it has passions, like individuals, and, like them, is prone to do wrong even while it sees what is right.

But the demagogues of Europe have made strange discoveries. According to them, a republic is not the rule of the majority, as has been thought until now, but the rule of those who are zealous partisans of the majority. It is not the people who predominate in this kind of government, but those who are best versed in the good qualities of the people. This is a happy distinction, which allows men to act in the name of nations without consulting them, and to claim their gratitude while their rights are trampled. A republican government, moreover, is the only kind that claims the right to do whatever it chooses and to despise what men have respected until now, from the highest moral obligations to the ordinary rules of common sense. Until our time it had been supposed that despotism was odious in whatever form it appeared. But it is a discovery of modern days that there is such a thing as legitimate tyranny and holy injustice, provided they are exercised in the name of the people.

The ideas the Americans have adopted about the republican form of government make it easy for them to live under it and ensure that it lasts. If in their country this form is often bad in practice, it is at least good in theory, and in the end the people always act in conformity with it.

It was impossible at the founding of the States, and it would still be difficult today, to establish a central administration in America. The inhabitants are scattered over too wide a space and separated by too many natural obstacles for one man to undertake to direct the details of their lives. America is therefore preeminently the country of local and municipal government. To this cause, which all the Europeans of the New World plainly felt, the Anglo-Americans added several others peculiar to themselves.

When the North American colonies were settled, municipal liberty had already made its way into the laws as well as the customs of the English, and the emigrants adopted it, not only as a necessity but as a benefit whose value they knew. We have already seen how the colonies were founded. Every province, and almost every district, was settled separately by men who were strangers to one another, or who had come together for very different purposes. The English settlers in the United States therefore saw early that they were divided into a great number of small, distinct communities that belonged to no common center. They saw that each of these little communities had to take care of its own affairs, since there seemed to be no central authority that was naturally bound, and easily able, to look after them. Thus the nature of the country, the way the British colonies were founded, the habits of the first emigrants, in short everything, combined to promote municipal and provincial liberties to an extraordinary degree.

In the United States, therefore, the great mass of the country’s institutions is essentially republican. To destroy permanently the laws that form the basis of the republic, it would be necessary to abolish all the laws at once. At the present day it would be even harder for a party to succeed in founding a monarchy in the United States than for a group of men to proclaim that France should from now on be a republic. Royalty would not find a body of legislation prepared for it in advance, and a monarchy would then exist surrounded, in fact, by republican institutions. The monarchical principle would likewise have great difficulty in making its way into the customs of the Americans.

In the United States, the sovereignty of the people is not an isolated doctrine unrelated to the prevailing customs and ideas of the people. On the contrary, it may be regarded as the last link in a chain of opinions that binds the whole Anglo-American world. That Providence has given every human being the degree of reason necessary to direct himself in the affairs that concern him alone is the great maxim on which civil and political society rests in the United States. The father of a family applies it to his children, the master to his servants, the township to its officers, the province to its townships, the State to its provinces, and the Union to the States. When it is extended to the nation, it becomes the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people.

Thus in the United States the fundamental principle of the republic is the same one that governs most human actions. Republican notions work their way into all the ideas, opinions and habits of the Americans, while they are formally recognized by the legislation, and before this legislation can be altered the whole community must undergo very serious changes. In the United States even the religion of most citizens is republican, since it submits the truths of the other world to private judgment, just as in politics the care of temporal interests is left to the good sense of the people. Thus every man is allowed to take freely the road he thinks will lead him to heaven, just as the law gives every citizen the right to choose his government.
It is evident that nothing but a long series of events, all tending the same way, can replace this combination of laws, opinions and customs with a mass of opposite opinions, customs and laws.

If republican principles are to perish in America, they can yield only after a laborious social process, often interrupted and as often resumed. They will have many apparent revivals, and they will not become completely extinct until an entirely new people has replaced the one that now exists. Now, it must be admitted that there is no symptom or sign that such a revolution is approaching. Nothing is more striking to a person newly arrived in the United States than the kind of tumultuous agitation in which he finds political society. The laws change incessantly, and at first sight it seems impossible that a people so changeable in its desires could avoid adopting a completely new form of government within a short time. Such fears are, however, premature. The instability that affects political institutions is of two kinds, which ought not to be confused. The first kind, which modifies secondary laws, is not incompatible with a very settled state of society. The other shakes the very foundations of the Constitution and attacks the fundamental principles of legislation. This kind of instability is always followed by troubles and revolutions, and the nation that suffers from it is in a state of violent transition.

Experience shows that the two kinds of legislative instability are not necessarily linked, since they have appeared together or separately depending on the time and the circumstances. The first is common in the United States, but the second is not. The Americans change their laws often, yet the foundation of the Constitution is respected.

Today the republican principle rules in America as the monarchical principle ruled in France under Louis XIV. The French of that time did not merely favor the monarchy; they could not imagine anything taking its place. They took it for granted, as we take the sun’s rays and the return of the seasons. Royal power had neither defenders nor opponents among them. In the same way, republican government exists in America without dispute or opposition, without proofs or arguments, by a tacit agreement, a sort of consensus universalis. Even so, it is my opinion that by changing their administrative forms as often as they do, the inhabitants of the United States put the future stability of their government at risk.

It may be feared that men, constantly thwarted in their plans by the changeability of the legislation, will come to regard republican institutions as an inconvenient form of society. The harm resulting from the instability of the secondary enactments might then raise a doubt about the nature of the fundamental principles of the Constitution and indirectly bring about a revolution. But that time is still very remote.

It may, however, be foreseen even now that when the Americans lose their republican institutions, they will quickly arrive at a despotic government, without a long interval of limited monarchy. Montesquieu remarked that nothing is more absolute than the authority of a prince who immediately succeeds a republic, since the powers that had been entrusted without fear to an elected magistrate are then transferred to a hereditary sovereign. This is true in general, but it applies more particularly to a democratic republic. In the United States the magistrates are not elected by a particular class of citizens but by the majority of the nation. They are the immediate representatives of the passions of the multitude, and since they depend wholly on its pleasure, they inspire neither hatred nor fear. Hence, as I have already shown, very little care has been taken to limit their influence, and they are left in possession of a vast amount of arbitrary power. This state of things has produced habits that would outlive it: the American magistrate would keep his power but would cease to be responsible for how he uses it, and it is impossible to say what limits could then be set to tyranny.

Some of our European politicians expect to see an aristocracy arise in America, and they already predict the exact time at which it will be able to take the reins of government. I have observed before, and I repeat, that the present tendency of American society appears to me to be toward ever greater democracy. I do not claim, nevertheless, that the Americans will never, at some future time, narrow the circle of political rights in their country, or confiscate those rights for the benefit of a single individual. But I cannot imagine that they will ever give the exclusive exercise of those rights to a privileged class of citizens, or, in other words, that they will ever found an aristocracy.

An aristocratic body consists of a certain number of citizens who, though not very far removed from the mass of the people, stand permanently above it. It is a body that is easy to touch and hard to strike. The people are in daily contact with it, yet can never unite with it. Nothing is more contrary to nature and to the secret leanings of the human heart than this kind of subjection, and men left to their own inclinations will always prefer the arbitrary power of a king to the regular administration of an aristocracy. Aristocratic institutions cannot last unless they make the inequality of men a fundamental principle, built into the legislation and affecting the condition of the human family as much as that of society. But such things are so repugnant to natural equity that they can be wrung from men only by force.

I do not think a single people can be cited, since human society began, that has by its own free will and its own exertions created an aristocracy within itself. All the aristocracies of the Middle Ages were founded by military conquest: the conqueror was the noble, and the conquered became the serf. Inequality was then imposed by force, and once it had been introduced into the customs of the country it sustained its own authority and was sanctioned by the legislation. There have been communities that were aristocratic from their earliest origin, owing to circumstances that preceded it, and that became more democratic with each succeeding age. Such was the fate of the Romans, and of the barbarians after them. But a people that began in civilization and democracy and that gradually established an inequality of conditions, until it arrived at inviolable privileges and exclusive castes, would be a novelty in the world, and nothing suggests that America is likely to furnish so singular an example.
Reflection on the Causes of the Commercial Prosperity of the United States

The Americans destined by Nature to be a great maritime people — Extent of their coasts — Depth of their ports — Size of their rivers — The commercial superiority of the Anglo-Americans, however, is less attributable to physical circumstances than to moral and intellectual causes — Reason for this opinion — Future destiny of the Anglo-Americans as a commercial nation — The dissolution of the Union would not check the maritime vigor of the States — Reason for this — The Anglo-Americans will naturally supply the needs of the inhabitants of South America — They will become, like the English, the commercial agents of a great part of the world.

The coastline of the United States runs more than two thousand miles, from the Bay of Fundy to the Sabine River in the Gulf of Mexico. These shores form one unbroken line, all under a single government. No nation in the world has larger, deeper or safer harbors for shipping than the Americans.

The inhabitants of the United States are a great civilized people whom fortune has placed in the midst of an uncultivated country, three thousand miles from the central point of civilization. America consequently needs European trade every day. The Americans will no doubt eventually succeed in producing or manufacturing at home most of the articles they require. But the two continents can never be independent of each other, so numerous are the natural ties between their needs, their ideas, their habits and their customs.

The Union produces distinctive commodities that have now become necessary to us but that cannot be grown in the soil of Europe, or can be raised there only at enormous expense. The Americans consume only a small portion of this produce, and they are willing to sell us the rest. Europe is therefore the market of America, as America is the market of Europe. Maritime commerce is no less necessary to enable the inhabitants of the United States to carry their raw materials to the ports of Europe than it is to enable us to supply them with our manufactured goods. The United States was therefore bound to face an alternative. If it had refused to enter into commerce itself, as the Spaniards of Mexico have so far done, it would have greatly increased the business of other maritime nations. The other course was to become one of the first trading powers of the globe.

The Anglo-Americans have always had a marked taste for the sea. The Declaration of Independence broke the commercial restrictions that bound them to England and gave a fresh, powerful boost to their maritime genius. Since then, the Union’s shipping has grown at nearly the same rapid pace as its population. Today the Americans themselves carry nine-tenths of the European goods they consume to their own shores. *g They also carry three-quarters of the New World’s exports to the European consumer. *h American ships fill the docks of Havre and Liverpool, while English and French vessels are comparatively few at New York. *i
