Thus the American merchant not only faces the competition of his own countrymen but also withstands that of foreign nations successfully in their own ports. This is readily explained by the fact that the vessels of the United States can cross the seas more cheaply than any other vessels in the world. As long as American merchant shipping keeps this superiority, it will not only hold on to what it has gained but will steadily grow more prosperous.

It is hard to say why the Americans can trade at a lower rate than other nations, and at first one is led to attribute this to physical or natural advantages within their reach. But that supposition is mistaken. American vessels cost almost as much to build as our own. *j They are not better built, and they generally last a shorter time. The pay of the American sailor is higher than the pay on board European ships, as is proved by the great number of Europeans to be found in the merchant vessels of the United States. But I am of the opinion that the true cause of their superiority must not be sought in physical advantages, and that it is wholly attributable to their moral and intellectual qualities.
j [ Materials are, generally speaking, less expensive in America than in Europe, but the price of labor is much higher.]

The following comparison will illustrate my meaning. During the campaigns of the Revolution, the French introduced a new system of tactics into the art of war, which bewildered the oldest generals and very nearly destroyed the most ancient monarchies in Europe. They undertook, as had never been attempted before, to do without a number of things that had always been held indispensable in warfare. They demanded new exertions from their troops, such as no civilized nation had ever thought of. They achieved great things in an incredibly short time, and they risked human life without hesitation to gain the object in view. The French had less money and fewer men than their enemies, and their resources were infinitely inferior. Nevertheless they were constantly victorious, until their adversaries chose to imitate their example.

The Americans have introduced a similar system into their commercial ventures, and they do for cheapness what the French did for conquest. The European sailor navigates with caution. He sets sail only when the weather is favorable. If an unforeseen accident befalls him, he puts into port. At night he furls part of his canvas, and when the whitening waves signal that land is near, he slows down and takes a reading of the sun. But the American neglects these precautions and braves these dangers. He weighs anchor in the midst of raging gales. By night and by day he spreads his sails to the wind. He repairs as he goes along whatever damage his vessel has suffered from the storm, and when he finally nears the end of his voyage, he darts on toward the shore as if he already saw a port. The Americans are often shipwrecked, but no trader crosses the seas as fast. And since they cover the same distance in a shorter time, they can do it at a lower cost.

The European stops several times at different ports in the course of a long voyage. He loses a good deal of precious time getting into harbor, or waiting for a favorable wind to leave it, and he pays daily dues for the right to remain there. The American sets out from Boston to buy tea in China. He arrives at Canton, stays a few days, and then returns. In less than two years he has sailed the entire circumference of the globe, and he has seen land only once. It is true that during a voyage of eight or ten months he has drunk brackish water and lived on salt meat, and that he has been in constant struggle with the sea, with disease and with the tedium of his existence. But on his return he can sell a pound of his tea for a halfpenny less than the English merchant, and his purpose is accomplished.

The best way I can explain my meaning is to say that the Americans bring a kind of heroism to the way they trade. The European merchant will always find it very hard to imitate his American rival. In following the system I have just described, the American is guided not only by a calculation of profit but by an impulse of his nature.

The inhabitants of the United States are subject to all the wants and desires that come with an advanced stage of civilization. But they are not surrounded, as Europeans are, by a community admirably equipped to satisfy those wants, and so they are often obliged to provide for themselves the various articles that education and habit have made necessities. In America it sometimes happens that the same person tills his field, builds his house, makes his tools, makes his shoes, and weaves the coarse cloth of which his clothing is made. This circumstance is harmful to the quality of the work, but it greatly helps to awaken the intelligence of the worker. Nothing tends more than an extreme division of labor to turn a man into a mere material thing and to strip his work of the faintest trace of mind. In a country like America, where men devoted to special occupations are rare, a long apprenticeship cannot be required of anyone who takes up a profession. The Americans therefore change their means of earning a living very readily, and they suit their occupations to the demands of the moment, in the way most profitable to themselves. One meets men who have been, in turn, lawyers, farmers, merchants, ministers of the gospel and physicians. If the American is less perfect in each craft than the European, there is at least scarcely any trade of which he is completely ignorant. His capacity is more general, and the range of his intelligence is wider.

The inhabitants of the United States are never bound by the axioms of their profession. They escape all the prejudices of their present station. They are no more attached to one line of work than to another, and no more inclined to use an old method than a new one. They have no deep-rooted habits, and they easily shake off the influence that the habits of other nations might have on their minds, out of a conviction that their country is unlike any other and that its situation has no precedent in the world. America is a land of wonders, in which everything is in constant motion and every movement seems an improvement. The idea of novelty is there inseparably connected with the idea of improvement. No natural boundary seems to be set to the efforts of man, and what is not yet done is only what he has not yet attempted to do.

This perpetual change that goes on in the United States, these frequent reversals of fortune, along with such unforeseen fluctuations in private and public wealth, keep the minds of the citizens in a constant state of feverish agitation. This admirably invigorates their efforts and keeps them in a state of excitement above the ordinary level of mankind. The whole life of an American is passed like a game of chance, a revolutionary crisis or a battle. Since the same causes are continually at work throughout the country, they ultimately give the national character an irresistible impulse. The American, taken as a random sample of his countrymen, must then be a man of unusual warmth in his desires, enterprising, fond of adventure, and above all fond of innovation. The same bent shows in everything he does. He brings it into his political laws, his religious doctrines, his theories of social economy and his domestic occupations. He carries it with him into the depths of the backwoods as well as into the business of the city. It is this same passion, applied to maritime commerce, that makes him the cheapest and the quickest trader in the world.

So long as American sailors keep these invigorating advantages and the practical superiority that comes from them, they will go on supplying the needs of the producers and consumers of their own country. They will also tend more and more to become, like the English, the commercial agents of every other people. *k This prediction has already begun to come true. We can see American traders making themselves intermediaries in the commerce of several European nations, *l and America will offer their enterprise a still wider field.

The great colonies founded in South America by the Spaniards and the Portuguese have since become empires. Civil war and oppression now lay waste those vast regions. The population does not increase, and the thinly scattered inhabitants are too absorbed in the cares of self-defense even to attempt any improvement of their condition. This, however, will not always be so. Europe has succeeded by her own efforts in piercing the gloom of the Middle Ages. South America has the same Christian laws and Christian customs as we have. She contains all the seeds of civilization that have grown among the nations of Europe or their offshoots, together with the advantages to be gained from our example. Why then should she always remain uncivilized? It is clear that the question is simply one of time. At some future period, more or less remote, the inhabitants of South America will form flourishing and enlightened nations.

But when the Spaniards and Portuguese of South America begin to feel the wants common to all civilized nations, they will still be unable to satisfy those wants for themselves. As the youngest children of civilization, they must of necessity admit the superiority of their elder brethren. They will be farmers long before they succeed in manufacturing or commerce, and they will need strangers to act as intermediaries in exchanging their produce overseas for the articles for which a demand will begin to be felt.

It is beyond question that the Americans of the North will one day supply the needs of the Americans of the South. Nature has placed them side by side. She has given the Northerners every means of knowing and understanding those needs, of establishing a permanent connection with those States, and of gradually filling their markets. An American merchant could lose these natural advantages only if he were far inferior to the European merchant, and he is in fact superior to him in several respects. The Americans of the United States already exert a very considerable moral influence on all the peoples of the New World. They are the source of enlightenment, and all the nations that inhabit the same continent are already accustomed to regard them as the best informed, the most powerful, and the wealthiest members of the great American family. All eyes are therefore turned toward the Union. The States that make it up are the models the other communities try to imitate as best they can, and it is from the United States that they borrow their political principles and their laws.

The Americans of the United States stand in exactly the same position toward the peoples of South America as their forefathers, the English, hold toward the Italians, the Spaniards, the Portuguese, and all those European nations that receive their everyday goods from England because they are less advanced in civilization and trade. England is at this time the natural trading center for almost all the nations within its reach. The American Union will play the same part in the other hemisphere. Every community that is founded, or that prospers, in the New World is founded and prospers to the advantage of the Anglo-Americans.

If the Union were dissolved, the commerce of the States that now compose it would undoubtedly be checked for a time, but this effect would be less noticeable than is generally supposed. It is clear that, whatever happens, the commercial States will remain united. They all border one another; they have exactly the same opinions, interests, and customs; and they alone are capable of forming a very great maritime power. Even if the South of the Union became independent of the North, it would still need the services of those States. I have already observed that the South is not a commercial country, and nothing suggests that it is likely to become one. The Americans of the South will therefore be obliged, for a long time to come, to turn to outsiders to export their produce and to supply them with the goods they need to meet their wants. But the Northern States can undoubtedly act as their middlemen more cheaply than any other merchants. They will therefore keep that business, for cheapness is the sovereign law of commerce. National claims and national prejudices cannot withstand the force of cheapness. Nothing could be more bitter than the hatred between the Americans of the United States and the English. Yet in spite of these hostile feelings, the Americans get the greater part of their manufactured goods from England, because England supplies them at a lower price than any other nation. Thus the growing prosperity of America, despite the grudges of the Americans, turns to the advantage of British manufactures.

Reason shows, and experience proves, that no commercial prosperity can last if it cannot be joined, when needed, to naval force. This truth is as well understood in the United States as anywhere else. The Americans are already able to make their flag respected; in a few years they will be able to make it feared. I am convinced that the breakup of the Union would not reduce the naval power of the Americans but would greatly help to increase it. At present the commercial States are tied to others that do not share their interests, and that often give reluctant consent to the growth of a maritime power from which they benefit only indirectly. If, on the contrary, the commercial States of the Union formed one independent nation, commerce would become the foremost of their national interests. They would therefore be willing to make very great sacrifices to protect their shipping, and nothing would prevent them from carrying out their plans on this point.

Nations, like individuals, almost always show the main features of their future in their earliest years. When I look at the energy with which the Anglo-Americans throw themselves into commercial enterprise, at the advantages that favor them, and at the success of their ventures, I cannot help believing that they will one day be the foremost maritime power on earth. They are born to rule the seas, just as the Romans were born to conquer the world.
